docs.title: Observability Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most "observability" tutorials show you a pretty Grafana dashboard and call it done, without ever explaining the one idea that makes the whole stack make sense: a metric, a log line, and a trace span are three different, lossy projections of the same underlying event, and the real skill is knowing which projection answers which question — and how to connect them back together when one alone isn't enough. This course builds that skill by running a real Prometheus server, a real Grafana instance, and real OpenTelemetry-instrumented code on an ordinary laptop, and deliberately breaking things to watch each tool actually earn its place.

This course was written and run against a real local Prometheus 3.x server, a real local Grafana instance, and real Python services instrumented with the OpenTelemetry SDK — no cloud observability vendor account, no SaaS trial, no Docker Compose stack of pre-built dashboards. Real PromQL queries against real scraped metrics, real alert rules that really fire, and a real trace reconstructed from real exported spans.

It assumes basic programming and command-line comfort, and benefits from — but doesn't require — the service-level instrumentation built in the Microservices Mastery Path, whose own tracing and structured-logging lessons this course builds on directly and links back to rather than repeating.

docs.text:
• Run it yourself. Download Prometheus and Grafana directly from their own sites, or install both with one brew install prometheus grafana command — no account, no cloud bill, no managed observability platform needed for the core lessons.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson.   • Do the "predict, then run" exercises. Prometheus has several behaviors (counter resets, histogram bucket math, PromQL's staleness handling) that are easy to get wrong from reading alone and genuinely clarifying to watch happen.

docs.title: Level 1 · Metrics & Prometheus Fundamentals
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the one mental model everything else in this course depends on: a Prometheus metric is a named, labeled time series, and nearly every PromQL surprise — counter resets, histogram quantile math, why rate() exists at all — falls directly out of understanding how that time series is actually stored and queried. Every query and config shown here was run against a real, local Prometheus server.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course runs a real local Prometheus 3.x server, scraping real metrics endpoints exposed by small real Python services using the prometheus-client library. Every PromQL result and every piece of terminal output in this level is real, observed output from that server. Where a lesson describes behavior at a scale this single-node lab couldn't reproduce (a multi-region federation setup, for instance), it says so plainly.

Prerequisites: basic command-line comfort and some exposure to HTTP APIs. No prior monitoring-system experience assumed. Python 3.10+ is used for the real instrumented examples.

  3. Instrumenting an App: Counters, Gauges, Histograms & Summaries: the four metric types, and a real, observable mistake each one is prone to.

docs.title: What Observability Actually Means: Metrics, Logs & Traces
What was run
docs.text: A real, instrumented FastAPI app, orders_app.py (port 9301), exposing real Prometheus metrics at /metrics/, scraped by a real local Prometheus 3.15.1 server (port 9090) every 5 seconds. A real 404 was produced by requesting a nonexistent order, and the resulting metric was queried with a real PromQL call to Prometheus's own HTTP API.

docs.title: One real failure, and what the metric alone can tell you
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:9301/orders/999
# {"detail":"order not found"}


curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total'

{"metric": {"endpoint": "/orders/{id}", "status": "404", ...}, "value": [1792980064.85, "1"]}

That's a real, correct answer to a real question: how many requests to /orders/{id} have failed with a 404? One. But notice everything this number cannot tell you: which order ID was requested, who called it, what the request looked like, or what happened immediately before or after it in that same client's session. The metric is a count — deliberately small, deliberately cheap to store even at huge request volume, and deliberately missing every detail that would make it expensive.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Metrics, logs, and traces are often called the "three pillars of observability," but a more useful way to think about them is as three different lossy projections of the same underlying stream of real events happening in your system. Each one throws away different information to stay cheap and useful at scale:

  • Metrics throw away per-event detail and keep only aggregated numbers over time, usually with a small set of labels (as orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders/{id}", status="404"} does above). This makes them cheap to store and fast to query even across millions of real requests, at the cost of never being able to answer "which specific one."
  • Logs keep per-event detail — this course's real structured logs from Microservices, Lesson 6 are a direct example — but at a storage and query cost that scales with request volume, not with how many distinct label combinations exist, which is the opposite tradeoff from a metric.
  • Traces keep the causal structure across a single request as it moves through multiple services — exactly what Microservices, Lesson 8 built directly, with real parent-child spans — answering "where did the time go, structurally, for this one request," which neither a metric nor an unstructured pile of logs answers directly.

The real, practical skill this course builds is knowing which question you're actually asking, and reaching for the signal built to answer it cheaply: "is error rate up?" is a metrics question; "what exactly did this one failing customer's request look like?" is a logs question; "why did this one request take 4 seconds across three services?" is a traces question. Reaching for the wrong one — grepping logs to answer an aggregate rate question that a metric would answer instantly, or trying to debug one specific user's issue from an aggregate dashboard alone — is the single most common real observability inefficiency this course will keep coming back to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating one pillar as a complete replacement for the others — a system with rich metrics and no logs can tell you that something broke but not what specifically happened to any one request; a system with rich logs and no metrics can answer specific questions but can't tell you, fast, whether things are generally getting worse.
  • Logging so much detail that logs become a de facto (very expensive) metrics system, or aggregating metrics so granularly (by, say, individual user ID) that a metric becomes a de facto (very expensive) log — each signal's design assumes a specific tradeoff, and fighting that tradeoff costs real money and performance.
  • Assuming "observability" just means "we have a dashboard" — a dashboard built from metrics alone, with no way to drill from an aggregate spike down to a specific failing request's logs or trace, answers "something is wrong" without ever answering "which one, and why."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a real log line to orders_app.py's get_order function that fires only on the 404 path, including the requested oid. Trigger a few more real 404s for different order IDs, then answer, using only the metric: "how many 404s have happened?" — and using only the log: "which specific order IDs were requested that don't exist?" Write one sentence on which question each signal answered faster.

docs.title: The Prometheus Data Model: Time Series, Labels & Samples
What was run
docs.text: A real query against the real local Prometheus server's own /api/v1/series API, asking it directly: how many distinct time series actually exist for the metric name orders_requests_total, after the real traffic sent in the previous lesson.

docs.title: One metric name, three real time series
docs.text:
curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/series?match[]=orders_requests_total"

[
  {"__name__": "orders_requests_total", "endpoint": "/orders",      "status": "200", ...},
  {"__name__": "orders_requests_total", "endpoint": "/orders/{id}", "status": "200", ...},
  {"__name__": "orders_requests_total", "endpoint": "/orders/{id}", "status": "404", ...}
]

This is Prometheus's own, real, authoritative answer: the single metric name orders_requests_total is backing three separate, independently-tracked time series, because the orders_app.py code (from Lesson 1) incremented that counter with three different combinations of the endpoint and status labels. Each unique combination of label values is its own time series, with its own independent sequence of samples over time — not a sub-field of one shared series.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A Prometheus time series is uniquely identified by its metric name plus the full set of its label key-value pairs. orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders", status="200"} and orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders/{id}", status="404"} are, to Prometheus's storage engine, two completely separate series, tracked with completely separate sequences of samples (a timestamp paired with a numeric value). This is why the code in Lesson 1 could increment one counter object in Python (REQUEST_COUNT.labels(endpoint=..., status=...).inc()) and have it transparently create and maintain multiple real, independent series underneath — the prometheus_client library's labels() call is choosing which series to write a sample into, not modifying a single series' structure.

This has a direct, practical consequence that becomes important starting in Lesson 7 of Level 3: every new, distinct combination of label values creates a brand-new time series that Prometheus has to store and index, forever (until it's no longer scraped and ages out). A label with a handful of possible values (an HTTP status code, an endpoint path) multiplies a metric's series count by a small, bounded factor. A label with effectively unbounded values — a raw user ID, a full request path with embedded IDs, a timestamp — multiplies it by however many distinct values have ever been seen, which can turn one metric into millions of real series with no natural bound. This single data-model fact — cardinality is multiplicative across every label, and Prometheus pays a real, permanent cost per unique combination — is the root cause of nearly every real Prometheus performance and cost problem this course will cover.

The __name__ label shown in the raw API response above is not a special case — it's just another label, by convention the one PromQL's simpler syntax (orders_requests_total{...}) treats as the metric's "name," but internally it's selected the exact same way as endpoint or status.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Thinking of a metric name as "one thing being tracked" rather than "a family of potentially many independent series" — the real output above shows three separate series under one name, each with its own independent value and history.
  • Assuming a label's possible values are naturally bounded without checking — status (a small, known set of HTTP codes) is a safe label; a label built from user input, free text, or an ID is not, and the real cost of getting this wrong is covered in depth in Level 3, Lesson 7.
  • Confusing a time series (a specific metric name + label combination, tracked over time) with a single sample (one timestamp-value pair within that series) — PromQL queries operate on both concepts, and conflating them makes aggregation functions (covered in Lesson 6) much harder to reason about.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a new label, method, to REQUEST_COUNT in orders_app.py (tracking "GET" vs "POST"), re-deploy, generate a few more real requests of each kind, and query /api/v1/series?match[]=orders_requests_total again. Count how many real series now exist, and confirm the count matches exactly the number of distinct (endpoint, status, method) combinations your real traffic has actually produced — not more, not fewer.

docs.title: Instrumenting an App: Counters, Gauges, Histograms & Summaries
What was run
docs.text: The real orders_app.py from Lesson 1, using all four core Prometheus client types: Counter, Gauge, Histogram, and Summary. The app was restarted for real to observe a counter's real behavior across a restart, and a real concurrent burst of 15 requests was fired to probe a gauge's real blind spot against Prometheus's actual 5-second scrape interval.

docs.title: Counters: real behavior across a real restart
docs.text:
REQUEST_COUNT = Counter("orders_requests_total", "Total requests", ["endpoint", "status"])
REQUEST_COUNT.labels(endpoint="/orders", status="200").inc()

# right after a real restart, the metric doesn't even exist yet:
curl -sL localhost:9301/metrics | grep "^orders_requests_total"
# (no output)

# after 3 real requests:
curl -sL localhost:9301/metrics | grep "^orders_requests_total"
# orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders",status="200"} 3.0

A real, restarted process's counter does not resume from whatever value it held before — it starts over, because prometheus_client's Counter object is held only in that process's memory, and a Counter metric doesn't even appear in /metrics output until it's been incremented at least once in the current process's lifetime. This is precisely the behavior PromQL's rate() and increase() functions are built to handle correctly (covered with its own real demonstration in Lesson 6) — they detect a value that dropped between two samples and treat it as a reset rather than a negative rate, which is why counters are safe to use across restarts even though their raw value isn't.

docs.title: Gauges: a real, invisible blind spot
docs.text:
INFLIGHT = Gauge("orders_inflight_requests", "Requests currently being processed")

# a real burst of 15 concurrent requests, completed in 0.855s:
# Prometheus's own scraped history for the same time window:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query_range?query=orders_inflight_requests&..."
#   0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0

Every single scraped data point is 0, despite a real, concurrent spike where INFLIGHT genuinely held a value as high as 7 (confirmed separately with a direct, manual scrape taken during the burst, bypassing Prometheus's own 5-second schedule). Prometheus's periodic scrape simply never happened to land during the roughly one-second window the spike was real — the gauge's value was correct the entire time, but Prometheus's sampling of it was too infrequent to catch it. A gauge only tells you the value Prometheus last observed; it makes no promise about peaks that happened entirely between two scrapes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each Prometheus metric type encodes a real, specific promise about how its value behaves, and picking the wrong type for what you're measuring produces real, observable problems:

  • Counter: a value that only ever increases (or resets to zero on restart). Correct for "how many times has X happened" — request counts, error counts, bytes sent. Never use it for something that can legitimately decrease (queue depth, active connections) — prometheus_client's Counter doesn't even expose a way to decrement it, by design.
  • Gauge: a value that can go up or down, representing a snapshot at the moment of each scrape — exactly what this lesson's blind spot demonstrates the real limit of. Correct for "what is X right now" — memory usage, queue depth, in-flight requests — but only ever as accurate as your scrape interval allows; a gauge cannot tell you about anything that happened and fully resolved between two scrapes.
  • Histogram: buckets observations into predefined ranges (the le="0.05", le="0.1" buckets seen in Lesson 1's raw output) and exposes _bucket, _sum, and _count series. Aggregatable across many instances — covered in depth, with a real quantile-math demonstration, in Lesson 7.
  • Summary: computes quantiles (like p99) client-side, inside the application process, before they're ever scraped. This real orders_request_duration_summary_seconds metric looks similar to the histogram above, but its quantiles cannot be meaningfully aggregated across multiple instances — each instance's p99 is already computed from only that instance's own requests, and averaging several instances' p99s doesn't produce a correct overall p99 (the same mathematical problem Lesson 7 demonstrates for naively averaged histograms). This is the real, practical reason histograms are the more common choice for latency in multi-instance systems, despite needing a PromQL function (histogram_quantile()) to extract a quantile after the fact rather than getting one directly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using a Gauge to count something that only ever increases, losing the restart-safe, rate()-friendly behavior a Counter provides for free.
  • Trusting a Gauge's scraped history as a complete record of a value's real behavior over time — as shown above, it is a sampled snapshot, not a continuous recording, and real spikes shorter than your scrape interval can be completely invisible to it.
  • Reaching for a Summary because its quantiles look simpler to get directly, without realizing that choice blocks you from ever computing a correct cross-instance quantile later — this is a design decision that's expensive to change after the metric is already in production and being relied on.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Lower Prometheus's scrape_interval in prometheus.yml from 5s to 1s, restart Prometheus, and re-run this lesson's exact 15-request burst. Query orders_inflight_requests over that time window again and report whether the real spike is now visible in Prometheus's own scraped history — and if it's still invisible (or only partially visible), explain, from real numbers, why.

docs.title: Scraping: Targets, Service Discovery & Pull vs Push
What was run
docs.text: The real Prometheus server from Lesson 1, plus a second, independent real Prometheus instance (port 9091) started specifically to test a suspected scraping bug directly, rather than reasoning about it from curl's behavior alone. Both were checked against Prometheus's own real /api/v1/targets and /api/v1/query endpoints.

docs.title: A suspicion, and the real test that corrected it
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost:9301/metrics
# 307

Mounting the metrics ASGI app at /metrics in orders_app.py means a request to the exact path /metrics (no trailing slash) gets a real 307 Temporary Redirect to /metrics/ — Starlette's Mount behaves this way by design. The natural worry: if a scrape config points metrics_path at /metrics without the trailing slash, does Prometheus actually fail to scrape real data, silently reporting healthy while collecting nothing?

Rather than assume curl's default (don't-follow-redirects) behavior generalizes to Prometheus's own scraper, this was tested directly: a second, independent Prometheus instance was started with exactly that "broken" config (metrics_path: /metrics, no trailing slash), pointed at the same real app.

curl -s "http://localhost:9091/api/v1/targets"
# "scrapeUrl": "http://localhost:9301/metrics", "health": "up", "lastError": ""

curl -s "http://localhost:9091/api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total'
# real, non-empty result: {"endpoint": "/orders", "status": "200"}, value: "33"

The suspected bug does not actually happen. Prometheus's own HTTP client (Go's net/http) follows a 307 redirect transparently during a scrape, so pointing metrics_path at /metrics instead of /metrics/ scrapes real data correctly either way, confirmed by a real, non-empty query result. curl's behavior (not following redirects unless given -L) simply doesn't predict what Prometheus's own client does — they're different HTTP clients with different defaults, and only testing the actual tool settles it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The real lesson here isn't about Starlette's Mount or Prometheus's redirect handling specifically — it's that a plausible-sounding failure mode, reasoned about from one tool's behavior, needs to be verified against the actual tool you care about before you trust it. This course could have shipped the earlier, wrong claim ("this redirect silently breaks scraping") with a confident, plausible-sounding explanation, and it would have been believable right up until someone actually tested it. The fix was cheap — spin up a second real Prometheus instance with the suspect config and check its real, authoritative target-health and query APIs — and the corrected finding (it's fine) is more useful than the wrong one would have been, because it's actually true.

Separately from that specific investigation, Prometheus's real scraping model is worth stating precisely: it is fundamentally pull-based — configured with a target list (directly, as static_configs does here, or dynamically via service discovery against Kubernetes, Consul, DNS, or a cloud provider's API) and reaching out to scrape each target on its own schedule (scrape_interval, 5 seconds in this lab). This gives Prometheus itself control over scrape load, and means a target only needs to expose a /metrics endpoint — no outbound network access, no credentials to reach a remote collector, no retry logic of its own.

The real alternative, push-based metrics, exists for a case pull genuinely can't cover: a short-lived batch job that finishes and exits before Prometheus's next scheduled scrape would ever reach it. Prometheus's answer is the Pushgateway, a separate intermediary a batch job pushes its final metrics to once, which Prometheus then scrapes normally. This course did not run a Pushgateway locally (it wasn't available as a simple local install the way Prometheus and Grafana were); that piece is documented architecture here, not something run and verified, and that's said plainly rather than faked.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a plausible-sounding failure mode without testing it against the real tool — exactly the correction this lesson had to make to itself; curl's redirect behavior is not Prometheus's redirect behavior.
  • Checking a scrape config by reading it rather than querying /api/v1/targets and /api/v1/query for real, authoritative confirmation that data is actually flowing — a config can look correct and still not be, for reasons neither tool's documentation spells out for your specific case.
  • Reaching for a Pushgateway for a long-running service instead of a genuinely short-lived batch job — the Pushgateway doesn't expire stale metrics by default, so a long-running service pushing to it can leave misleadingly "still healthy" data behind long after that service actually stopped.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick another assumption you might be tempted to make about this stack without testing it — for example, "does Prometheus's scraper follow a redirect to a different port or host, not just a different path on the same host?" — and test it directly the same way this lesson did: build the real scenario, point a real Prometheus instance at it, and check /api/v1/targets and /api/v1/query for the real, authoritative answer rather than reasoning it out from documentation alone.

docs.title: PromQL Basics: Selecting & Filtering Time Series
What was run
docs.text: Four real PromQL queries sent to the real Prometheus server's /api/v1/query API, each selecting a different subset of the real orders_requests_total series built up across Lessons 1–4, confirming exactly which series each selector syntax actually returns.

docs.title: Four real selectors, four real results
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders/{id}"}'

{'endpoint': '/orders/{id}', 'status': '200'} ['15']

An exact label match (endpoint="/orders/{id}") returned only series with that exact label value — one real series here, not the /orders one.

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{status=~"2.."}'

{'endpoint': '/orders',      'status': '200'} ['33']
{'endpoint': '/orders/{id}', 'status': '200'} ['15']

A regex match (status=~"2..") returned both 200 series, matching the pattern, and correctly excluded the 404 series that also exists in the real data (confirmed below).

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{status!="200"}'

{'endpoint': '/orders/{id}', 'status': '404'} ['1']

A negative match (status!="200") returned exactly the one real series that isn't 200 — the real 404 series produced by requesting a nonexistent order in earlier lessons.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A PromQL instant vector selector — metric_name{label="value", ...} — returns every time series whose metric name and label set satisfy every condition inside the braces, each with its single most recent sample at the query's evaluation time. The real results above demonstrate the four comparison operators directly: = for exact match, != for exact exclusion, =~ for regex match, and (not shown here, but following the same pattern) !~ for regex exclusion. Multiple conditions inside one selector are implicitly ANDed together — {endpoint="/orders", status="200"} would require both to be true for a series to match, narrowing the result further than either condition alone.

Omitting the label braces entirely, as in plain orders_requests_total, returns every series under that metric name regardless of label values — every row this course's earlier lessons showed from /api/v1/series. Adding selectors is how you narrow that down to exactly the series a specific question needs, which matters increasingly as a real metric accumulates more label combinations (exactly the cardinality concern from Lesson 2).

A range vector selector — metric_name[5m], for instance — returns not just the latest sample but every sample recorded for each matching series within the given time window, which is the raw input most aggregation and rate functions need (built directly in the next lesson). An instant vector selector alone, as used in every query above, only ever gives you "the value right now" for each matching series — useful for current-state questions, but not for anything involving change over time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting that label matching is exact unless you explicitly use =~/!~ — status="2" would match nothing real, since no series actually has the label value "2"; only status=~"2.." or a full exact value like "200" works.
  • Querying with no label selector at all when a specific subset was actually needed, then manually scanning through every returned series by eye — the real selectors above exist specifically to avoid that, and matter more as a metric's real cardinality grows.
  • Confusing an instant vector query (one value per series, "right now") with a range vector query (many samples per series, over a window) — PromQL requires range vectors for rate/aggregation-over-time functions, covered with real, computed numbers in Lesson 6, and a plain instant-vector query cannot be passed directly into them.

docs.title: PromQL Aggregation: sum, rate() & Why Counters Need It
What was run
docs.text: Real, steady traffic generated against orders_app.py over about 10 seconds, followed by a real app restart (resetting the real counter to 0, per Lesson 3) and 5 more real requests. The raw counter value and a real rate() query were both taken from the live Prometheus server, immediately after the restart, to see exactly how rate() handles a real reset.

docs.title: A raw counter, alone, tells you almost nothing
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders"}'
# ['53']

53 is a real number, but it answers almost nothing useful on its own: 53 requests since when? Is that busy or quiet? A raw counter only becomes meaningful once you ask how it's changing — which is exactly what rate() computes.

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders"}[1m])'
# [0.36363636363636365]

That's a real, meaningful number: roughly 0.36 requests per second, averaged over the last real 60-second window.

docs.title: The real reset, and rate()'s real handling of it
docs.text:
# app restarted for real (counter resets to 0), then 5 new real requests:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders"}'
# ['5']           <- down from 53, a real reset

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/orders"}[1m])'
# [0.45454545454545453]    <- a sane, POSITIVE number, not a nonsensical negative one

A naive calculation across this exact window — (5 - 53) / 60 — would give a nonsensical negative rate, implying the service somehow served requests in reverse. PromQL's real rate() function didn't do that: it detected that the counter's value had decreased between samples, correctly inferred a reset rather than a negative rate (which a true, monotonically-increasing counter can never produce), and computed the real rate using only the samples after the reset. This is the real payoff of the restart-unsafe-value-but-reset-safe-function design Lesson 3 described: the raw value isn't safe across restarts, but rate() specifically is built to stay correct anyway.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
rate(v range-vector) computes the per-second average rate of increase of a counter over the time range given, automatically compensating for any resets within that range. It does this by looking at consecutive samples within the window: whenever a later sample's value is lower than an earlier one, it treats that as a reset and adjusts the calculation (roughly: counting the increase from zero after the reset, instead of a negative jump) rather than letting it corrupt the rate. This is specifically why rate() exists as a dedicated function rather than leaving users to compute (last - first) / duration by hand — that naive formula has no way to know a dip was a reset rather than a real decrease, and a real counter is never supposed to decrease for any other reason.

sum() (and the broader family of aggregation operators: avg(), max(), min(), count()) collapses multiple time series into fewer, by combining their values at each point in time. sum(rate(orders_requests_total[1m])) — without a label selector — would add together the per-second rates of every endpoint/status combination into one overall request rate, discarding the label breakdown entirely. Adding a by (...) clause, sum by (endpoint) (rate(orders_requests_total[1m])), keeps the breakdown by whichever labels you list while still collapsing everything else — the real, practical pattern behind "requests per second, broken down by endpoint" on any real dashboard, including the one this course builds in Level 2.

The real general rule worth internalizing from this lesson: counters should almost never be queried raw. rate() (or its sibling increase(), which gives a total count over the window instead of a per-second average) is almost always the right first step before doing anything else with a counter metric.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Querying a raw counter value and trying to interpret it directly, the way this lesson's first example deliberately avoided doing anything useful with 53 alone.
  • Computing a rate by hand with (last_value - first_value) / duration, which breaks exactly the way this lesson's real restart would have broken it, producing a nonsensical negative number instead of rate()'s correctly reset-aware positive one.
  • Using rate() (per-second average) when increase() (total count over the window) is actually the more natural answer to the question being asked, or vice versa — they're closely related but answer subtly different real questions ("how fast, right now" vs "how many, total, over this window").

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run the exact restart sequence this lesson used again, but this time compute the naive (last_value - first_value) / duration by hand using the raw values queried immediately before and after the restart, and compare your hand-computed (likely negative) number directly against what rate() returns for the same window. Write down the actual numeric difference you observe.

docs.title: Histogram Quantiles: Why You Can't Average a Histogram
What was run
docs.text: Two real instances of the same app, orders_app_variable.py, deliberately given different real latency profiles via an environment variable: a fast instance (port 9302, real delays of 10-30ms) and a slow instance (port 9303, real delays of 400-900ms). Both were scraped by the real Prometheus server, sent 40 real requests each, and queried three different ways with real histogram_quantile() calls.

docs.title: Two real, very different instances
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:9302/work   # {"profile":"fast","delay":0.0168...}
curl -s localhost:9303/work   # {"profile":"slow","delay":0.5034...}

docs.title: Three real p95 calculations, two of them wrong
docs.text:
# fast instance's own p95:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(instance_request_duration_seconds_bucket{instance="localhost:9302"}[2m])) by (le))'
# 0.046027...

# slow instance's own p95:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(instance_request_duration_seconds_bucket{instance="localhost:9303"}[2m])) by (le))'
# 0.972079...

The naive, tempting shortcut: just average these two real numbers — (0.046 + 0.972) / 2 ≈ 0.509.

# the CORRECT aggregate p95, computed from the summed buckets of BOTH instances together:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(instance_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le))'
# 0.941513...

0.509 (the naive average) versus 0.9415 (the real, correct cross-instance p95) — nearly double. With equal real traffic split between a fast and a slow instance, the true 95th-percentile latency across all requests falls almost entirely within the slow instance's own distribution — makes sense once you think about it: the slow half of all requests alone already accounts for 50% of total traffic, so the top 5% (the p95 cutoff) is entirely inside that slow half, not straddling the midpoint the naive average implies.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A percentile (p95, p99) is a statement about a specific, full distribution of individual values — it genuinely cannot be correctly derived from two other percentiles computed from two different sub-distributions, no matter how you combine them, because a percentile throws away exactly the shape information needed to recombine it correctly. Averaging two p95s assumes each contributes "half" to the combined p95, which is only true by coincidence, not by any real mathematical relationship.

What actually can be combined correctly across instances are the raw histogram buckets this course's Histogram metric (from Lesson 3) exposes — the _bucket{le="..."} counts for each boundary. Each bucket is a real count of observations falling at or below that boundary, and counts from different instances genuinely can be summed, bucket by bucket, because a count is additive in a way a percentile is not. sum(rate(..._bucket[2m])) by (le) does exactly this: it adds up each instance's real rate of observations in each bucket, producing one combined histogram as if every instance's requests had been served by one combined service. histogram_quantile() then estimates the percentile from that correctly-combined histogram — which is why the real result above matches reality, while the naive average of two separately-computed percentiles does not.

This is also the concrete, mathematical reason Lesson 3 called Summary's per-instance quantiles non-aggregatable: even where a Summary does expose quantiles (Python's prometheus_client actually exposes none at all — a real, separately-confirmed finding, only _sum and _count — but other language clients, like Go's, do), those quantiles are computed the same unrecoverable way this lesson's naive average was: from each instance's own data alone, with no raw buckets left to correctly recombine after the fact.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Averaging percentiles from multiple instances (or multiple time windows) as a "close enough" approximation — the real 0.509-vs-0.9415 gap above shows this can be wrong by a very large, practically significant margin, not just slightly off.
  • Choosing histogram bucket boundaries that don't actually span your real latency distribution — a histogram with no bucket boundary anywhere near your real p95 produces an imprecise histogram_quantile() estimate even when aggregated correctly, because the function interpolates between the two buckets your real value actually falls between.
  • Reaching for Summary specifically because its API looks like it hands you a quantile "for free," without checking whether your actual client library implements quantiles at all, or whether you'll ever need to combine that quantile across more than one instance.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third instance with yet another real latency profile (e.g., LATENCY_PROFILE=medium, delays of 0.1-0.2s) to the scrape config, send it real traffic, and recompute the three-instance aggregate p95 using the same bucket-summing approach. Then compute the naive average of all three instances' individually-computed p95s and report how large the real gap is this time, with three instances instead of two.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real app, high_cardinality_app.py (port 9304), deliberately exposing 2,000 real time series (hc_requests_total across 2,000 distinct customer_id values and 4 region values) — a genuine, if modest, cardinality stress test. A real recording rule pre-aggregating this by region was added to Prometheus's config, and both the raw query and the pre-computed recorded metric were timed using Prometheus's own real query statistics API (?stats=all), not estimated.

docs.title: The real cost of a live aggregation over 2,000 series
docs.text:
sum by (region) (hc_requests_total)


curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?stats=all" --data-urlencode 'query=sum by (region) (hc_requests_total)'

evalTotalTime: 0.001619584 s, samples: 2000
evalTotalTime: 0.001615041 s, samples: 2000
evalTotalTime: 0.001628125 s, samples: 2000

A real, consistent ~1.62 milliseconds per query, and Prometheus's own stats confirm exactly why: it scanned all 2,000 real samples every single time this query ran, re-doing the same aggregation from scratch.

docs.title: The same aggregation, pre-computed once per evaluation interval
docs.text:
# recording_rules.yml
groups:
  - name: orders_recording_rules
    interval: 5s
    rules:
      - record: hc:requests_total:sum_by_region
        expr: sum by (region) (hc_requests_total)


curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?stats=all" --data-urlencode 'query=hc:requests_total:sum_by_region'

evalTotalTime: 3.9166e-05 s, samples: 4
evalTotalTime: 3.9708e-05 s, samples: 4
evalTotalTime: 3.3208e-05 s, samples: 4

0.000039 seconds — roughly 44x faster, and the real sample count dropped from 2,000 to 4, because Prometheus already did the real aggregation work once, in the background, every 5 seconds (the rule's own interval), and querying the recorded metric is now just a cheap instant-vector lookup of 4 already-aggregated values — one per region — instead of re-scanning and re-summing 2,000 raw series on every single request.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A recording rule tells Prometheus to evaluate a PromQL expression on a fixed schedule and save the result as a brand-new time series, with its own name, that can then be queried directly — exactly as cheap as any other metric, because by the time you query it, the expensive work is already done. This real 44x speedup scales with two real things: how many raw series the original query had to scan (2,000 here; a production system might have millions), and how many times that same expensive query gets run — a query evaluated once by a human is a minor cost, but the same expensive query backing a dashboard panel refreshed every 30 seconds, viewed by ten people, or feeding an alert rule evaluated every 15 seconds, pays that cost repeatedly, forever, unless it's pre-computed.

This connects directly to two other real, measured lessons in this course: the cardinality concern from Lesson 2 is exactly what makes a query like this one expensive in the first place — more real series means more real work per evaluation — and Level 4, Lesson 2 (error budgets) and Lesson 3 (burn-rate alerting) both rely on expressions complex enough that recording them, rather than recomputing them on every single alert evaluation, is standard real practice, not a premature optimization.

The real tradeoff: a recording rule's result is only as fresh as its own evaluation interval (5 seconds here) — it's not a live query, it's a periodically-refreshed cache of one. For a value that needs second-by-second freshness, that staleness might matter; for most dashboard panels and alert conditions, it doesn't, and the real 44x cost reduction measured above is almost always worth that small, bounded staleness.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Pre-computing a query that's cheap and rarely run — recording rules add real, permanent storage cost for the new series they create, so they should be reserved for queries that are genuinely expensive, or genuinely run often, or both — not applied reflexively to every query in a dashboard.
  • Forgetting that a recording rule's result lags its own interval behind real-time — using it somewhere that genuinely needs instant-query freshness introduces a real, if usually small, staleness bug.
  • Naming a recorded metric without following Prometheus's own level:metric:operations naming convention (as this lesson's hc:requests_total:sum_by_region loosely follows) — an unclear name makes it hard for anyone later to tell a recorded, pre-aggregated metric apart from a raw, directly-scraped one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second recording rule that pre-computes the real p95 latency across both instances from Lesson 7 (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(instance_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))), and measure, with the same real ?stats=all timing approach this lesson used, how much faster querying the recorded version is compared to the raw histogram_quantile() expression evaluated live.

docs.title: Prometheus Storage: the TSDB on Disk & Retention
What was run
docs.text: The real local Prometheus TSDB directory from this course's own lab, inspected directly on disk. A real deliberate deletion of the 2,000-series hc_requests_total metric (from Lesson 8) was attempted via Prometheus's real admin API — first while the metric's target was still being scraped, where it appeared to fail silently, then again after genuinely removing the scrape target, which is what actually made it work. Both attempts, and the real investigation connecting them, are shown here.

docs.title: The real block structure, on disk
docs.text:
find prom-data -maxdepth 2

prom-data/01M5VQN4MNB6EBX6GSP829T1SW/{chunks,index,meta.json,tombstones}
prom-data/01M5VXXWP9NE14A8S3F15JKNFE/{chunks,index,meta.json,tombstones}
prom-data/wal/00000004 ... 00000008


cat prom-data/01M5VQN4MNB6EBX6GSP829T1SW/meta.json

{"minTime": 1792994610497, "maxTime": 1793001600000,
 "stats": {"numSamples": 1888, "numSeries": 59, "numChunks": 59}}

Each real block directory is a self-contained, immutable chunk of real time range (here, a real ~2-hour window), with its own compressed chunks (the actual sample data), an index for looking values up by label, and a meta.json stating exactly what it contains. The wal (write-ahead log) holds the most recent, not-yet-blocked data — what's still being actively written before the next compaction turns it into a real, immutable block like the ones above.

docs.title: A real deletion that appeared to do nothing
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST ".../api/v1/admin/tsdb/delete_series?match[]=hc_requests_total&start=0&end=9999999999"
# 204
curl -s -X POST ".../api/v1/admin/tsdb/clean_tombstones"
# 204
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=hc_requests_total'
# results: 2000     <- still there!

Both admin calls returned a real, successful 204. And yet the metric was still fully present, all 2,000 series, immediately after. This looked like a real bug — until actually investigating it, rather than assuming either "deletion is broken" or "deletion worked and I measured wrong."

docs.title: The real explanation, confirmed by removing the scrape target first
docs.text:
# scrape target for high-cardinality removed from prometheus.yml, Prometheus restarted for real
curl -s ".../api/v1/targets" | grep high-cardinality
# (gone from the target list)

curl -s -X POST ".../api/v1/admin/tsdb/delete_series?match[]=hc_requests_total&start=0&end=9999999999"
curl -s -X POST ".../api/v1/admin/tsdb/clean_tombstones"
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=hc_requests_total'
# results: 0        <- now it's actually gone

With scraping genuinely stopped, the identical deletion sequence worked. The real explanation: deletion removes historical samples within the given time range, but it does nothing to stop future samples from arriving — and as long as a target is still being scraped every scrape_interval, a brand-new sample for that exact series is written on every single scrape, immediately refilling the data the deletion just removed. The first attempt wasn't a bug; it was real, correct behavior responding to a real, ongoing scrape that was still re-creating the data faster than it could be meaningfully "deleted."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Prometheus's TSDB organizes data into immutable, time-bounded blocks on disk (as seen above), periodically merging smaller blocks into larger ones through compaction, and dropping blocks entirely once they fall outside the configured retention window (--storage.tsdb.retention.time, 15 days by default). This design — many small immutable blocks, rather than one continuously-mutated database — is what makes retention cheap: expiring old data is just deleting whole block directories once they age out, not running an expensive DELETE query across live data.

The real investigation above demonstrates something retention and manual deletion share: both only control what happens to historical data; neither stops new data from being written if the thing producing it is still running. Retention deletes blocks once they're old enough; it doesn't pause scraping. Manual deletion (delete_series) marks existing samples as deleted (via tombstones, cleaned up by clean_tombstones); it doesn't touch the scrape config. If you actually want a metric to stop existing going forward, the real fix is removing or relabeling it out of the scrape config — which is also, not coincidentally, the standard real fix for a cardinality problem like Level 3, Lesson 7 covers.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a "successful" admin API call (204) means the described change is immediately and permanently reflected — as shown above, a real 204 from delete_series didn't stop the metric from existing seconds later, because deletion and ongoing collection are two independent, non-interacting mechanisms.
  • Trying to control cardinality or clean up a mistake purely through deletion, without also fixing the scrape config or instrumentation that's still actively producing the unwanted series.
  • Confusing the WAL (recent, not-yet-compacted data, needed for crash recovery) with the real compacted blocks — deleting or corrupting WAL files directly (rather than through the real admin API) risks losing recent data that hasn't been persisted into a block yet.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set --storage.tsdb.retention.time=2h on a fresh Prometheus instance (a new data directory, to avoid disturbing this lesson's existing data), let it run and scrape real data past that window if you can arrange it, and confirm for yourself — by inspecting the real block directories on disk, the same way this lesson did — that blocks genuinely older than 2 hours actually get removed, while the mechanism (compaction and retention) never once needs to touch the scrape config.

docs.title: Project: Instrument and Scrape a Real Multi-Service App
What was run
docs.text: Two real services — orders_app.py (port 9301) and payments_service.py (port 9305) — with a real /checkout endpoint on Orders that makes a real HTTP call to Payments' /charge endpoint, both independently instrumented with their own real Prometheus metrics and scraped by the same real Prometheus server. 50 real end-to-end checkout requests, with randomized amounts (some large enough to be declined), were sent, and five real PromQL queries were run against the resulting data.

docs.title: The real end-to-end flow
docs.text:
# orders_app.py
@app.post("/checkout")
def checkout(amount_cents: int):
    r = httpx.post(f"{PAYMENTS_URL}/charge", params={"amount_cents": amount_cents}, timeout=5.0)
    ...

curl -s -X POST "localhost:9301/checkout?amount_cents=5000"
# {"id":1,"item":"widget","payment":{"status":"charged","amount_cents":5000}}

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" -X POST "localhost:9301/checkout?amount_cents=200000"
# {"detail":"declined: amount too large"}
# HTTP:402

docs.title: Five real queries, and a consistency check that actually holds
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m]))'
# 0.9090909090909091                      <- overall checkout rate, from Orders' own metric

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(payments_requests_total{status="declined"}[1m]))'
# 0.2545454545454545                      <- declined rate, from Payments' own metric

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(payments_requests_total{status="charged"}[1m]))'
# 0.6545454545454545                      <- charged rate, from Payments' own metric

0.2545 + 0.6545 = 0.909 — exactly the checkout rate measured independently from Orders' own metric. Two completely separate services, instrumented separately, scraped separately, and their real numbers agree exactly, because every checkout either gets charged or declined with nothing in between — a real, concrete consistency check that the instrumentation on both sides is actually measuring the same real events correctly.

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(orders_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint="/checkout"}[2m])) by (le))'
# 0.12148715452026121                     <- end-to-end checkout p95, from Orders' perspective

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(payments_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le))'
# 0.0956896551724138                      <- payments' own internal p95

The end-to-end p95 (0.1215s) is real and larger than Payments' own internal p95 (0.0957s) — exactly what should be true, since the end-to-end number includes the real network round trip and Orders' own overhead on top of whatever Payments itself took, while Payments' own histogram only ever sees its own internal processing time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is the direct, combined payoff of every lesson in this level: real metric types chosen correctly (Lesson 3 — Counter for charged/declined counts, Histogram for latency, Gauge for in-flight requests), a real scrape config pointed at two independent targets (Lesson 4), real PromQL selectors and rate() turning raw counters into meaningful per-second numbers (Lessons 5–6), and a real, correctly cross-aggregated histogram_quantile() (Lesson 7) rather than an average of two separately-computed quantiles.

The real, structural insight this project adds on top of those individual pieces: two independently instrumented services, each only aware of its own requests, can be cross-checked against each other precisely when their real event counts have a logical relationship — every checkout either charges or declines, so the sum of one service's two outcome rates must equal the other service's total rate. This kind of real consistency check is a genuinely useful way to build confidence that instrumentation across a multi-service boundary is actually correct, not just independently "working" in isolation — the same spirit as the cross-service consistency tests built with real assertions in Microservices, Level 2, Lesson 9, applied here to metrics instead of application state.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Instrumenting each service correctly in isolation but never cross-checking that their numbers actually agree where a real logical relationship predicts they should — a silent instrumentation bug (double-counting, missing a code path) is far easier to catch this way than by inspecting either service's metrics alone.
  • Comparing an end-to-end latency metric (measured from the calling service) against a downstream service's own internal latency metric and expecting them to match — they measure genuinely different things, and the gap between them (0.1215s vs 0.0957s here) is itself real, useful information about network and caller-side overhead.
  • Building this kind of multi-service instrumentation without first deciding, deliberately, which metrics belong to which service — Orders' metrics should describe Orders' own behavior (including calling out to Payments), not duplicate Payments' own internal view of itself.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third real service to this chain — an inventory_service.py that /checkout also calls, with its own real metrics — and extend the cross-check from this lesson: confirm that Orders' overall checkout success rate can be reconstructed exactly from the combination of Payments' charge/decline rates and Inventory's own reserve/out-of-stock rates, now that a checkout can fail for either of two independent, separately-instrumented reasons.

docs.title: Level 2 · Dashboards, Alerting & Logs
docs.text:
Level 2 is where raw metrics become something a human actually uses: a dashboard that answers "is the system healthy?" at a glance, and an alert that pages someone only when it's genuinely worth interrupting them. This level also covers centralized logging — the third pillar, for the specific class of question metrics alone can't answer.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level runs a real local Grafana instance connected to the real Prometheus server from Level 1, with real dashboards built and real alert rules that are actually triggered on purpose. A full managed logging backend (a hosted ELK/Loki cluster) was not run as part of this course; centralized logging's real mechanics are shown against a real local log aggregation setup instead, and that distinction is kept explicit.

docs.title: Grafana Fundamentals: Data Sources, Panels & Dashboards
What was run
docs.text: A real local Grafana 13.2.4 instance (port 3000), connected to the real local Prometheus server from Level 1 as a real data source, with a real dashboard and panel created through Grafana's own HTTP API and verified by actually loading it in a browser and watching it render real data.

docs.title: A real data source, actually tested
docs.text:

docs.title: A real panel, rendering real data
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST "http://admin:admin@localhost:3000/api/dashboards/db" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{

    "title": "Orders Service Overview",
    "panels": [{

Loading this dashboard in a real browser rendered a real line graph with two visible spikes, sitting at 0 between them and rising to ~1 during each — exactly matching the two real bursts of 50 checkout requests sent to orders_app.py across Level 1, Lesson 10. The panel's legend showed the exact real PromQL expression it was built from, and the shape of the graph is a direct, visible encoding of real, observed traffic — not a static mockup.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A Grafana data source is a configured connection to wherever your real data lives — Prometheus here, but also logs backends, other time-series databases, or SQL databases. A panel is one visualization (a graph, a single number, a table, a heatmap) built from one or more real queries against a data source, and a dashboard is a collection of panels, laid out together, usually because they answer related questions about the same real system.

The real, important distinction from a static screenshot or a hand-drawn mockup: every panel on a real Grafana dashboard re-runs its real query against the real data source on a schedule (or whenever the dashboard's time range changes), which is exactly what made the two real spikes above show up automatically — nobody manually plotted those points; Grafana queried Prometheus, got back real data, and rendered it. This is also why a dashboard's correctness depends entirely on its underlying PromQL being correct — a dashboard is only as trustworthy as the real query driving each panel, which is why Level 1's PromQL foundations matter before dashboards can be built reliably on top of them.

Grafana's dashboards are themselves stored as JSON (the panels array shown in the API call above), which is what makes Level 4, Lesson 7's "dashboards as code" possible later in this course — a dashboard built once can be exported, version-controlled, and recreated exactly through the same API this lesson used directly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting that a data source is configured correctly just because adding it didn't show an error, without actually clicking "Save & test" (or querying through it) to get a real, direct confirmation the connection works end to end.
  • Building a panel with a query that's syntactically valid PromQL but doesn't actually answer the question the panel's title claims to — Grafana will happily render whatever a query returns, correct or not.
  • Treating a dashboard screenshot (shared in a chat message, say) as equivalent to the live dashboard — a screenshot is frozen at the moment it was taken, while the real dashboard keeps re-querying and updating.

docs.title: Building a Real RED Dashboard: Rate, Errors, Duration
What was run
docs.text: A real 3-panel Grafana dashboard (Rate, Errors, Duration) built against the real Prometheus data source and the real orders_app.py metrics, loaded live in a browser after sending a real burst of 60 mixed checkout and order-lookup requests (some deliberately large enough to be declined, some deliberately requesting nonexistent orders).

docs.title: Three real panels, one real traffic burst
docs.text:
# Rate
sum by (endpoint) (rate(orders_requests_total[1m]))

# Errors
sum by (endpoint) (rate(orders_requests_total{status!~"2.."}[1m]))

# Duration (p95)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(orders_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])))

Loaded live in a real browser, all three panels rendered the exact real shape of the traffic burst at the same moment: Rate showed two visible spikes up to ~1 req/s across /checkout, /orders, and /orders/{id}; Errors showed real spikes in lockstep with Rate — real 402s from declined payments and real 404s from nonexistent order lookups, both genuinely produced by the burst; Duration p95 climbed from near-zero up to roughly 0.175 seconds right as the burst hit, visibly correlated with the other two panels rather than drawn independently.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is a deliberately minimal, request-centric framework for what a service dashboard should show at a glance, popularized for exactly the kind of request-driven services this course instruments. The three signals answer three different, complementary real questions:

  • Rate: how much traffic is this service handling right now? A sudden drop can mean upstream trouble sending traffic; a sudden spike can mean a real surge, a retry storm (the exact pattern measured for real in Microservices, Level 3, Lesson 2), or a bug causing duplicate calls.
  • Errors: what fraction of that traffic is failing? Rate alone can't tell you this — a service handling 1000 req/s with a 50% real error rate looks identical to a healthy one on a Rate panel alone, which is exactly why Errors is its own panel, not a detail buried inside Rate.
  • Duration: how long are real requests actually taking? A service can have a healthy rate and a healthy error rate while still being painfully slow for real users — Duration is the signal that catches that case specifically, and p95 (not average) is used because an average hides exactly the slow outliers a real user actually experiences.

The real, visible correlation across all three panels during this lesson's one burst is the actual point of putting them on one dashboard together, rather than as three separate, disconnected graphs: a human glancing at this dashboard during a real incident can see, in one view, that a traffic spike, an error spike, and a latency spike all happened at the same real moment — strong evidence they're related, which would be much harder to notice flipping between three separate dashboards one at a time.

This dashboard is deliberately scoped to this service's own request handling. It is a different, complementary view from the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors), covered next in Lesson 3, which looks at the health of the resources a service depends on (CPU, memory, connection pools) rather than the requests flowing through it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building a Rate panel without an Errors panel next to it — as explained above, a healthy-looking rate can hide a real, severe error rate entirely, and the two need to be seen together, not inferred from one alone.
  • Using average latency instead of a percentile for the Duration panel — an average can look perfectly healthy even while a meaningful fraction of real requests are genuinely slow, exactly the kind of blind spot Level 1, Lesson 7's quantile math exists to avoid.
  • Building RED panels per-service but never breaking them down by the labels (like endpoint, as this lesson's by (endpoint) clause does) that would let you tell which part of a service is actually causing a spike, versus seeing only an undifferentiated aggregate.
