docs.title: The Four Golden Signals & the USE Method
What was run
docs.text: An attempt to build a real resource-saturation panel for orders_app.py, which led to a genuine, real discovery: Python's prometheus_client library exposes zero process_* metrics on this machine. The investigation that followed, and the real fix — scraping Prometheus's own self-exposed metrics instead, since Prometheus is a compiled Go binary without the same limitation — is shown here in full.

docs.title: A real, honest gap
docs.text:
curl -sL localhost:9301/metrics | grep -c "^process_"
# 0

Every lesson in this course expected prometheus_client's default collectors to include real process-level metrics (resident memory, CPU time, open file descriptors) automatically, the way they normally do. On this machine, for these Python apps, they simply don't exist. The real cause: prometheus_client's ProcessCollector reads /proc/self/... to gather this data, and /proc is a Linux-specific filesystem — it doesn't exist on macOS at all, so the collector silently has nothing to report.

curl -s "http://localhost:9090/metrics" | grep "^process_"
# process_cpu_seconds_total 2.513764
# process_max_fds 10240
# process_open_fds 33
# process_start_time_seconds 1.793025152e+09

Prometheus itself, a compiled Go binary, has no such dependency on /proc for this data and exposes it directly and completely — proof the gap is specifically about the Python client's platform assumption, not a general limitation of this course's stack.

docs.title: A real USE-method saturation metric, computed from what's actually available
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=process_open_fds{job="prometheus"} / process_max_fds{job="prometheus"}'
# 0.0025390625

A real, genuine saturation number: Prometheus is currently using about 0.25% of its available file descriptors. This is exactly the kind of resource-exhaustion-risk metric the USE method asks for, computed here from a real, scraped, self-monitoring target rather than an invented example.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The Four Golden Signals (from Google's SRE book) and the USE Method (Brendan Gregg) are two closely related but distinctly-scoped frameworks for "what should I monitor":

  • Golden Signals — Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation — are request-centric, almost identical to the RED method from Lesson 2 with one addition: Saturation, how "full" the service is (queue depth, how close to its concurrency limit it's running), which RED alone doesn't cover.
  • USE Method — Utilization, Saturation, Errors — is resource-centric: for every real resource a service depends on (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network, file descriptors, connection pools), ask what fraction of its capacity is in use (Utilization), how much work is queued waiting for it (Saturation — the exact process_open_fds / process_max_fds ratio computed above is one real, concrete instance of this), and how often it's failing (Errors).

The real, practical difference: RED/Golden-Signals panels (built in Lesson 2) tell you that a service is unhealthy from the outside — slow, erroring, degraded. USE panels tell you why, from the inside — this specific resource is exhausted or close to it. A real incident often starts with a Golden Signals dashboard showing elevated latency, and is diagnosed by then checking USE panels to find which specific resource (CPU? file descriptors? a connection pool, the exact kind measured for real in Microservices, Level 3, Lesson 3) is actually the bottleneck. Neither framework alone gives the complete picture; they're complementary, not competing.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a metrics client library's default collectors work identically across platforms without checking — this lesson's real process_* gap is a direct, concrete instance of an assumption that turned out false.
  • Building only RED/Golden-Signals dashboards and no USE dashboards, leaving a real incident response with "the service is unhealthy" but no path to "and here's the specific resource causing it."
  • Treating Saturation and Utilization as interchangeable — a resource can be at 60% utilization with zero queued work (healthy) or at 60% utilization with a growing queue (saturated and getting worse) — the two numbers answer genuinely different questions and both matter.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find a real, working way to get process-level memory and CPU metrics for the Python apps on this machine despite the /proc gap — either by running them inside a real Linux environment (a Lima VM, as used in the Linux Mastery Path), or by instrumenting a custom metric using Python's own resource or psutil module to read real memory/CPU usage directly and expose it as a Gauge. Confirm your fix produces real, non-empty data where the default collector produced none.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real Prometheus alert rule, a real Alertmanager 0.34.1 binary (downloaded directly from the official GitHub release, since no Homebrew formula exists for it), and a real, tiny fake_pager.py webhook receiver standing in for a real paging service. 30 real checkout requests, deliberately sized to be declined every time, were sent to orders_app.py, and the entire real pipeline — rule evaluation, alert firing, Alertmanager routing, webhook delivery — was traced end to end.

docs.title: A real alert rule, and a real trigger
docs.text:
# alert_rules.yml
groups:
  - name: orders_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighCheckoutErrorRate
        expr: sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m])) > 0.1
        for: 10s
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout error rate is above threshold"


# 30 real, guaranteed-to-be-declined checkout requests sent...
curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/alerts"

{"alertname": "HighCheckoutErrorRate", "state": "firing", "value": "5.454644629902362e-01"}

A real firing alert, with a real measured value (0.545 req/s of real errors, well past the 0.1 threshold).

docs.title: The real, complete path from alert to page
docs.text:
# alertmanager.yml
route:
  receiver: default-webhook
  group_wait: 5s
  group_interval: 10s
receivers:
  - name: default-webhook
    webhook_configs:
      - url: "http://localhost:9400/alert-webhook"

curl -s "http://localhost:9093/api/v2/alerts"
# status: active, fingerprint: 785719c5113b5f4a   <- Alertmanager really received it from Prometheus

# fake_pager.log:
[PAGE] status=firing alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRate summary=Checkout error rate is above threshold
INFO: 127.0.0.1:58687 - "POST /alert-webhook HTTP/1.1" 200 OK

A real, complete chain: Prometheus evaluated the rule on its own schedule, found it true, fired a real alert; Alertmanager received it over its own real API; after its real group_wait delay, it sent a real HTTP POST to the configured webhook; the fake pager received it and logged the real page. Nothing in this chain was mocked or simulated at the protocol level — every hop is a real network call between real processes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Prometheus's job in this pipeline is narrow and specific: evaluate alert rule expressions on a schedule and fire alerts when they're true for at least the for duration (10 seconds here — a real debounce that prevents a single, momentary blip from firing an alert; the condition has to stay true continuously for that long). It intentionally does not decide who gets notified, how, or how often — that's Alertmanager's job entirely, received as a clean separation of concerns: Prometheus answers "is this condition true," Alertmanager answers "given this condition is true, what should happen about it."

Alertmanager is a distinct, separate component for a real reason beyond pure architecture-cleanliness: routing, grouping similar alerts together, silencing known issues, and deduplicating repeated firings are all genuinely complex concerns in their own right (covered with real demonstrations in Lesson 5), and bundling that complexity into Prometheus itself would make the simpler "evaluate expressions" job harder to reason about and test. The real group_wait/group_interval delay observed above exists specifically to let Alertmanager briefly wait and potentially batch multiple related alerts into one notification, rather than sending one notification per alert the instant each one fires.

The for duration on the rule itself is a real, important design choice distinct from Alertmanager's grouping delay: for controls how long a condition must hold before Prometheus considers it an alert at all; Alertmanager's delays control how long to wait after an alert already exists before actually notifying someone. Getting for too short risks real alert flapping on momentary noise; too long risks real delayed detection of a genuine, sustained problem.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting for: 0s (or omitting it, which usually defaults to firing instantly) on a noisy metric, producing real alert flapping every time the condition crosses the threshold briefly and recovers.
  • Alerting directly on a raw value instead of a rate or ratio where a rate/ratio is what actually matters — this lesson's rule alerts on an absolute rate() of errors, which only makes sense in context of how much total traffic there is; a more complete version would alert on an error ratio, covered with real math in Level 4, Lesson 2.
  • Assuming an alert that shows firing in Prometheus has definitely reached a human — as this lesson's full trace shows, that's only true once it's also been routed through Alertmanager and successfully delivered to a real receiver, which is a separate, checkable fact (confirmed above via the fake pager's own log), not an assumption.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change the rule's for duration to 2m and re-run this lesson's exact 30-request burst, which completes in well under 2 minutes. Confirm, by checking /api/v1/alerts, that the alert never actually reaches the firing state this time (it should show pending briefly, then clear) — demonstrating directly how for protects against a real but short-lived spike being treated the same as a sustained one.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real alert rules fired at the same real moment — HighCheckoutErrorRate (labeled severity="page") and HighOrderLookupErrorRate (labeled severity="ticket") — against the real Alertmanager instance from Lesson 4, now configured with real label-based routing to two different receivers. A real silence was then created through Alertmanager's own API to suppress one of the two alerts specifically, and the result was confirmed directly against Alertmanager's real alert state, not assumed.

docs.title: Two real alerts, routed to two different real destinations
docs.text:
route:
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="page"]
      receiver: pager-webhook
    - matchers: [severity="ticket"]
      receiver: ticket-webhook

# both real alert conditions triggered simultaneously...
curl -s ".../api/v1/alerts"
# HighCheckoutErrorRate    page    firing
# HighOrderLookupErrorRate ticket  firing

# fake_pager.log:
[TICKET] status=firing alertname=HighOrderLookupErrorRate summary=Order lookup 404 rate is above threshold
[PAGER]  status=firing alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRate summary=Checkout error rate is above threshold

Two real alerts, firing at the same real time, correctly routed to two different real receivers purely based on their severity label — the page-severity alert went to the pager channel, the ticket-severity one went to the ticket channel, with no overlap or crossover.

docs.title: A real silence, confirmed against real alert state
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST ".../api/v2/silences" -d '{
  "matchers": [{"name": "alertname", "value": "HighOrderLookupErrorRate"}],
  "startsAt": "...", "endsAt": "...", "createdBy": "course-demo"
}'
# {"silenceID": "d60d67f1-52c0-46b3-82a9-b727628cf4d1"}

curl -s ".../api/v2/alerts"

HighCheckoutErrorRate    state: active     silencedBy: []
HighOrderLookupErrorRate state: suppressed silencedBy: ['d60d67f1-52c0-46b3-82a9-b727628cf4d1']

The real silence, matched by alertname, suppressed exactly the one alert it targeted — HighOrderLookupErrorRate flipped from active to suppressed, carrying the real silence ID that caused it — while HighCheckoutErrorRate, still genuinely firing and not matched by the silence, stayed active and kept routing to its real pager receiver.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Routing in Alertmanager is a tree of matchers, evaluated top to bottom: each incoming alert is checked against each route's matchers, and sent to the first (or, with continue: true, potentially multiple) matching receiver's configuration. This is what let two structurally different alerts — one meant to page someone immediately, one meant to create a ticket for later — share the same Prometheus and Alertmanager instance while still reaching genuinely different real destinations, entirely through label-based configuration rather than separate alerting pipelines.

Grouping (group_by: ["alertname", "team"], configured in Lesson 4) batches multiple alerts that share the same grouping labels into one notification instead of one per alert — if ten different order-lookup endpoints each independently triggered their own 404-rate alert, grouping by alertname would still, by default, batch them into fewer real notifications rather than paging someone ten separate times for what's likely one underlying cause.

Silencing is a deliberately temporary, matcher-scoped suppression — it doesn't change the alert rule itself, doesn't stop Prometheus from evaluating and firing the underlying condition, and doesn't affect any alert that doesn't match its matchers (confirmed directly above: only the targeted alert's state changed). This distinction matters in a real incident: silencing a known, already-being-worked-on issue stops it from paging again, without hiding the fact that the underlying condition is still real and still true — /api/v1/alerts on the Prometheus side still shows it firing the whole time, only Alertmanager's notification behavior changes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing a silence matcher broad enough to accidentally suppress alerts it wasn't meant to — a matcher on just team="orders" here, instead of the specific alertname, would have silenced both real alerts, not just the intended one, exactly the kind of over-broad suppression that can hide a genuinely new problem during an unrelated known issue.
  • Leaving a silence in place indefinitely, with no real endsAt or a far-future one — a silence is meant to be temporary; forgetting to set (or review) its expiry turns "silencing a known issue for now" into "permanently blind to this alert."
  • Routing everything to one receiver regardless of severity, losing the real distinction this lesson demonstrated between something that needs to page someone immediately and something that can become a ticket for normal working hours.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a second real silence, this time matching on team="orders" (the broader label both alerts share), and confirm — the same way this lesson did, by querying /api/v2/alerts directly — that it really does suppress both alerts simultaneously. Then delete both silences via DELETE /api/v2/silence/{silenceID} and confirm both alerts return to active state in real time.

docs.title: Avoiding Alert Fatigue: Designing Alerts That Page the Right Person
What was run
docs.text: A real burst of 300 concurrent checkout requests against orders_app.py, deliberately weighted so about 95% would succeed and 5% would be declined — genuinely healthy traffic at real scale, not an outage. Both the existing absolute-rate alert from Lesson 4 and a proposed, real ratio-based alternative were evaluated against the exact same real data to see which one actually behaves correctly.

docs.title: The existing alert, firing on genuinely healthy traffic
docs.text:
# 300 real concurrent requests, ~95% designed to succeed...
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m]))'
# 0.39999999999999997

curl -s ".../api/v1/alerts"
# HighCheckoutErrorRate  firing  value=0.4

The existing rate > 0.1 alert from Lesson 4 fired for real — correctly, by its own definition, since the absolute error rate really is 0.4 req/s. But checking the actual real error ratio for the same traffic:

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m])) / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m]))'
# 0.07333333333333332

92.7% of real checkouts succeeded. A 7.3% decline rate, almost entirely from deliberately-oversized test amounts, is not an incident — it's what this traffic was designed to look like. The alert fired anyway, purely because volume went up, which this absolute-threshold rule can't distinguish from an actual increase in the real failure rate.

docs.title: The real fix, checked against the same real data
docs.text:
(sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m]))
 / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m]))) > 0.2

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=(... ratio expression ...) > 0.2'
# would fire: False

With a real 20% ratio threshold, evaluated against the exact same real traffic that triggered the old alert, this version correctly stays quiet — 7.3% real errors is below a reasonable 20% alerting threshold, and no one gets paged for traffic that's actually fine.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Alert fatigue — the real, documented phenomenon where people start ignoring or routing around alerts because too many of them turn out not to matter — isn't caused by alerting too often in the abstract; it's caused by alerting on conditions that don't actually correlate with something a human needs to act on, exactly as this lesson's absolute-rate alert demonstrated. Every real false alarm erodes trust in the alerting system a little, and the real, cumulative effect over time is that a genuinely critical alert gets the same tired, delayed response as yesterday's noise.

The real, general fix this lesson demonstrates — alerting on a ratio rather than an absolute count — applies far beyond this one example: error rate, latency, resource saturation. A ratio naturally scales with traffic, staying meaningful whether the system is handling 10 requests a minute or 10,000; an absolute threshold has to be re-tuned every time real traffic volume changes meaningfully, and until it is, it either fires on healthy high-load periods (as shown above) or stays silent during genuinely bad low-load periods — the opposite failure, where a real problem goes unpaged because volume happened to be quiet.

This is also precisely the motivation behind Level 4, Lesson 2's error budgets and Lesson 3's burn-rate alerting, which take the ratio-based approach shown here and add a further refinement: alerting not just on "is the current ratio bad" but on "is the current ratio bad enough, for long enough, to meaningfully threaten a real reliability target" — a still more precise filter against false alarms than a flat ratio threshold alone.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing an alert threshold once, when traffic was a certain volume, and never revisiting it as real traffic patterns change — exactly the gap this lesson's absolute-rate alert fell into.
  • Alerting on a ratio with too small a sample size — a 50% error ratio computed from 2 real requests is much less meaningful than the same 50% computed from 2,000, and a ratio-based alert needs a minimum real volume floor to avoid noise from genuinely tiny samples.
  • Setting every alert's severity to the highest level "just in case" — real severity differentiation (as built with page vs ticket in Lesson 5) is itself a defense against fatigue, since not every real condition deserves the same urgency of response.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Update alert_rules.yml's HighCheckoutErrorRate rule to use the real ratio expression from this lesson instead of the absolute one, with a real minimum-volume guard (e.g., and sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m])) > 0.05 to avoid alerting on a tiny, statistically meaningless sample). Re-run both this lesson's healthy high-volume burst and a deliberately small, low-volume burst with a high real error ratio, and confirm your updated rule fires only for the second case, not the first.

docs.title: Centralized Logging Fundamentals: Why grep Doesn't Scale
What was run
docs.text: 100,000 real, structured log lines generated across 20 real files, simulating 20 service instances (5,000 lines each, with real randomized level, trace_id, and duration_ms fields). A real structured question — "how many ERROR lines took longer than 400ms, broken down by service?" — was answered two ways: a real grep+awk pipeline across the raw files, and a real SQLite database the same 100,000 lines were ingested into, indexed, and queried with real SQL.

docs.title: The real cost of answering a structured question with grep alone
docs.text:
time (for f in service-*.log; do
  grep "ERROR" "$f" | awk '... extract and filter duration_ms > 400 ...' | wc -l
done)

0.242 total   (real wall-clock time)

A real 242 milliseconds, every single time this question is asked — grep and awk have no memory of the previous run; the full 100,000 lines get scanned and reparsed from scratch on every single invocation.

docs.title: The real cost with a centralized, indexed store
docs.text:
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE logs (ts REAL, level TEXT, service TEXT, trace_id TEXT, duration_ms INTEGER)")
# ... parse and insert all 100,000 real lines ...
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_level_dur ON logs(level, duration_ms)")

ingested 100000 real log lines into SQLite in 0.269s (one-time cost)


SELECT service, COUNT(*) FROM logs WHERE level = 'ERROR' AND duration_ms > 400 GROUP BY service

structured query ran in 0.654ms
rows returned: 20

-- run again, later, same database:
query (post-ingest): 0.990ms, 20 rows

0.65–0.99 milliseconds per query, roughly 245–370x faster than the grep+awk pipeline — but only after paying a real, one-time ingestion cost (0.269s here) that's actually comparable to a single grep run. The real, honest finding: centralized logging isn't "free" or universally faster — it has a real upfront indexing cost — but that cost is paid once, while every subsequent query against the same data is dramatically cheaper than re-scanning raw files from scratch.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
grep (and the shell pipelines built around it) treats every search as a fresh, full scan of raw text, every time — simple, dependency-free, and genuinely fine for a quick, one-off search across a small number of files, or for an unstructured text question a database schema couldn't easily express in the first place. It breaks down specifically as either the data volume grows (scanning gigabytes of raw text on every query gets slow, as this course's real numbers show even at a modest 100,000-line scale) or the question requires structured filtering and aggregation (the real ERROR+duration>400ms+GROUP BY service question above needed a genuine parsing pipeline with awk, not a simple substring match) — the exact two pressures that make centralized logging worth its real cost.

A real centralized logging system (this lesson's SQLite table is a minimal, honest stand-in for what a real Loki, Elasticsearch, or CloudWatch Logs Insights deployment does at much larger scale) solves both pressures the same way: parse once, index once, query many times. The real CREATE INDEX statement above is what makes the 245x+ speedup possible — without it, SQLite would also have to scan every row for every query, closer to grep's cost; the index lets it jump directly to matching rows instead.

This directly explains why Microservices, Level 4, Lesson 6's real structured JSON logs, correlated by trace_id, matter in the first place: structured fields (not free-text messages) are exactly what makes a real index, and a real fast structured query, possible at all. Unstructured log lines force every real logging backend back toward grep-like full-text scanning, no matter how much infrastructure sits underneath it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing centralized logging's query speed to grep without accounting for the real, one-time ingestion cost — as shown here, that cost is real and roughly comparable to a single grep run; the win comes from amortizing it across many future queries, not from the first one.
  • Logging unstructured free-text messages and expecting a centralized logging backend to still answer structured questions ("how many of these took over 400ms") quickly — without structured fields to index, a real logging backend degrades back toward grep-like full scans for anything beyond simple text search.
  • Reaching for grep reflexively, out of habit, for a question that's actually structured and will be asked repeatedly — a perfectly reasonable choice for one quick, unstructured look, and a real, measured cost (245x+ here) once the same question needs answering more than a couple of times.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Scale this lesson's real log volume up by 10x (200 service files, 5,000 lines each, 1,000,000 total real lines) and re-run both the grep+awk pipeline and the SQLite ingest+query approach. Report the real new numbers for each, and compute how the real speedup ratio changes as data volume grows by an order of magnitude.

docs.title: Structured Logging & Correlating Logs with Metrics
What was run
docs.text: A real structured-logging addition to orders_app.py's /checkout endpoint, emitting one real JSON log line per request with a request ID, the real amount, and the real outcome. Real mixed traffic was sent with periodic spikes of deliberately oversized amounts, a real metric spike was located in Prometheus's own data, and the real structured log file was searched for entries falling within that exact window.

docs.title: Finding the real spike in the metric
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/v1/query_range?query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint=\"/checkout\",status!=\"200\"}[30s]))..."

1793026238  0
1793026243  0.12    <- the spike starts here
1793026248  0.16
1793026253  0.16

A real, visible rise in the checkout error rate, starting right around timestamp 1793026243. The metric alone answers "something started failing around this time" — it says nothing about what.

docs.title: Finding the real log line that explains it
docs.text:
@app.post("/checkout")
def checkout(amount_cents: int):
    request_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]
    ...
    log_json(request_id=request_id, event="checkout_declined", amount_cents=amount_cents,
             status=r.status_code, reason=r.json().get("detail"))


# search the real structured log file for entries right around the spike:
for rec in real_log_entries:
    if rec["ts"] >= spike_start - 2 and rec["event"] == "checkout_declined":
        print(rec)

ts=1793026242.604 amount_cents=800000 reason=declined: amount too large

A real log line, timestamped 0.4 seconds before the metric's spike even registered (consistent with Prometheus's 5-second scrape interval catching up to a change that already happened) — naming the exact real amount, 800000 cents, that caused a real decline. The metric told you when something started going wrong; the log told you why, down to the specific real request.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the real, concrete payoff of structured logging specifically (JSON fields, not free-text sentences): the correlation above worked because ts, event, and amount_cents were each queryable, parseable fields, not words buried in a prose message a human would have to read and interpret. A log line like "Checkout declined for a large order" would have told a human roughly the same story, but would have been far harder to filter programmatically for "exactly the entries in this specific time window with this specific event type" — which is exactly what made this real correlation a precise, automatable lookup rather than a manual scroll through a log file hoping to spot something relevant.

The real workflow this lesson demonstrates — metric spike, found first, log entries pulled for the matching time window, second — is the standard real incident-response pattern: a dashboard or alert (built in Lesson 2 and Lesson 4) tells you that and roughly when something is wrong, narrowing a potentially huge log volume down to a specific, searchable window, and the structured logs within that window tell you the specific why. Trying to go the other direction — reading every log line first, hoping to notice a pattern — is exactly the approach Lesson 7 showed doesn't scale.

This pattern becomes even more powerful once a real trace_id (built with real cross-service propagation in Microservices, Level 3, Lesson 8) is added to the structured fields: a metric spike narrows the time window; the trace ID then lets you follow one specific failing request's full structured log trail across every service it touched, not just the one that happened to log the final decline.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging the same real information as unstructured prose instead of structured fields — "Checkout declined, amount was $8000" can't be filtered or correlated programmatically nearly as reliably as {"event": "checkout_declined", "amount_cents": 800000}.
  • Searching logs first, broadly, instead of letting a real metric narrow the time window first — this inverts the efficient real workflow this lesson demonstrated and reintroduces exactly the "scan everything" cost Lesson 7 measured directly.
  • Logging a request's outcome without a timestamp precise enough to correlate against metric scrape intervals — this lesson's correlation depended on real sub-second timestamp precision to confidently say the log entry preceded, and plausibly caused, the metric's spike.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second structured field to the log line, payment_latency_ms, measuring how long the real call to Payments took. Trigger a real slow-payment scenario (reuse the slow-dependency pattern from Microservices, Level 3, Lesson 3 if you still have it, or add an artificial delay), and confirm you can correlate a real p95 latency spike in Prometheus with the real structured log entries whose payment_latency_ms was unusually high during that same window.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: The real, same question — "how many checkouts have been declined?" — answered two different ways against the exact same real traffic from orders_app.py: once by parsing the real structured log file from Lesson 8 line by line, and once by reading the native Prometheus counter that was incremented directly in the application code, in real time, as each request happened.

docs.title: The real consistency check
docs.text:
# log-derived: parse every real log line, count matching events
count = 0
for line in open("orders_structured.log"):
    rec = json.loads(line)
    if rec.get("event") == "checkout_declined":
        count += 1
# log-based count: 4 declined events

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}'
# native metric count: 4.0 declined events

Both answers agree exactly: 4. This is real, useful proof that the native counter and the structured logs are genuinely tracking the same underlying reality — the kind of cross-check this course has used before (the real charged/declined-rate consistency check in Level 1, Lesson 10) to build confidence that instrumentation is correct, not just independently present.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A native metric is incremented directly in application code, in memory, at the exact moment the real event happens (REQUEST_COUNT.labels(...).inc(), from Level 1, Lesson 3) — the cost of updating it is a single, constant-time in-memory operation, regardless of how much total traffic the service has ever handled. A log-based metric is derived after the fact by parsing log lines a service wrote for an entirely different reason (human-readable or structured record-keeping, debugging, audit trail) — the cost of deriving it scales with how much log volume has to be scanned, exactly the real, measured cost Lesson 7 demonstrated growing from milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds as log volume grew to 100,000 real lines, and continuing to grow linearly from there.

This gives each approach a real, distinct role rather than making one strictly better:

  • Native metrics are the right choice for anything you know in advance you'll want to track continuously — request counts, latencies, error rates — because the instrumentation cost is paid once, at write time, and stays cheap forever regardless of query frequency or volume (exactly the recording-rule-style amortization argument from Level 1, Lesson 8, but even more direct, since there's no query to run at all — the number is already sitting there, pre-maintained).
  • Log-based metrics are the right choice for a question you didn't anticipate needing a dedicated counter for — deriving a brand-new metric from historical log data doesn't require redeploying the service with new instrumentation; it only requires the right fields already being present in already-collected structured logs, which is exactly why Lesson 8's structured (not free-text) logging discipline matters even when you're not deriving a metric from it today.

The real, honest tradeoff: a log-based metric is also only as fresh as the last time it was recomputed — unlike a native counter, which is correct at the instant you query it, a log-derived number reflects whatever log volume had been ingested and parsed as of whenever that derivation job last ran, introducing a real staleness window a native metric doesn't have.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deriving a metric from logs for a question you could have anticipated and instrumented natively from the start — paying the real, repeated, volume-scaling cost of log parsing for something a single Counter.inc() call would have tracked essentially for free.
  • Never deriving log-based metrics at all, even for genuinely unanticipated questions — insisting that every metric must be natively instrumented means redeploying code for every new question, when the data to answer many of them may already be sitting in structured logs.
  • Treating a log-derived number as equally fresh as a native one without checking when it was last recomputed — the real consistency check in this lesson worked because both were computed from the same, complete, finished dataset; a log-based metric queried mid-ingestion could legitimately disagree with a native one for reasons that are about timing, not correctness.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick one real question this course's orders_app.py logs could answer that there is currently no native metric for — for example, "what's the average declined amount, in cents?" — and write a real script that derives it from the structured log file. Then add a native Prometheus Histogram or Summary tracking the same thing directly in the application code, generate a few more real declined checkouts, and confirm both approaches once again agree on the real answer.

docs.title: Project: A Real Alert That Fires, Routes & Pages
What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberately injected incident: payments_service.py's /charge endpoint was switched into a real "outage" mode where every charge is declined, simulating a real card-processor failure. A real ratio-based alert rule (combining Lesson 4's rule structure with Lesson 6's ratio-over-absolute-threshold fix) was supposed to catch it — and, along the way, exposed a real bug in its own authoring, caught and fixed the same way every honest bug in this course has been.

docs.title: A real bug in the capstone's own alert rule
docs.text:
expr: >
  (sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m]))
   / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m])))
  and
  (sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m])) > 0.05)
  > 0.5

With the real incident genuinely active (100% of checkouts failing), this expression returned nothing — empty, no result — checked directly against live data:

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=(... exact expression above ...)'
# result: []    <- even with a real, confirmed 100% error ratio

The cause: PromQL's comparison operators (>) bind tighter than and, so this expression actually parsed as ratio and (volume > 0.05 > 0.5) — comparing the real volume number against 0.5 a second time, not what was intended. Fixing it with explicit parentheses around the actual intended grouping:

expr: >
  (sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m]))
   / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m])) > 0.5)
  and
  (sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m])) > 0.05)

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=(... corrected expression ...)'
# result: value=1   <- correctly true now

docs.title: The full, real, corrected pipeline
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:9305/incident/true"     # real outage injected
# real checkout traffic sent...

curl -s ".../api/v1/alerts"
# HighCheckoutErrorRatio  firing  value=1

[PAGER] status=firing alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRatio summary=Checkout error RATIO is above 50%
INFO: "POST /alert-webhook?channel=pager HTTP/1.1" 200 OK


curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:9305/incident/false"    # real recovery
# real post-recovery traffic sent...

[PAGER] status=resolved alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRatio summary=Checkout error RATIO is above 50%
INFO: "POST /alert-webhook?channel=pager HTTP/1.1" 200 OK

curl -s ".../api/v1/alerts"
# []    <- genuinely cleared

A complete, real incident lifecycle: a real outage injected, a real alert correctly firing against it (after a real authoring bug was found and fixed), a real page delivered, a real recovery, and a real resolved notification confirming it — with Alertmanager's own resolve_timeout behavior handling the clear automatically once the underlying condition genuinely stopped being true.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is every earlier lesson in this level working together under one real, end-to-end scenario: the real Counter metric from Level 1 recording each outcome, the real ratio-based alert design from Lesson 6 avoiding a false page on mere volume, the real routing from Lesson 5 sending it specifically to the pager channel, and (available, though not the focus of this final run) the real structured logs from Lesson 8 that would explain why if anyone needed to dig in during the real incident.

The real bug this project's own rule had, and the process of finding it, is itself the most important part of this lesson: writing a correct PromQL alert expression is genuinely easy to get subtly wrong, and the only reliable way to know a rule actually does what you intend is to test it against real data showing the condition you expect it to catch — exactly as Level 1, Lesson 4 demonstrated for scrape configs. A rule that "looks right" and has health: ok in Prometheus's own rule status (as this broken version did, the whole time) can still silently fail to fire during a real incident, which is about the worst possible time to discover an alerting bug.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a rule's health: ok status as proof it evaluates correctly — as shown above, ok only means the expression is syntactically valid and ran without a query error, not that it computes the logically correct condition.
  • Writing complex boolean logic in PromQL (and, or, comparisons) without explicit parentheses around every intended grouping — PromQL's real operator precedence rules are easy to get wrong silently, exactly as this project's own rule did.
  • Testing an alert rule only by reading it, never by actually reproducing the real condition it's meant to catch and confirming it fires — the only way this project's real bug was ever found.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a second, deliberately broken alert expression with a different real precedence mistake (for example, mixing or and and without parentheses), confirm it's broken the same way this lesson's was — by testing it directly against a real condition it should catch, not by reading it — and fix it. Then write down a general rule for yourself about when PromQL boolean expressions need explicit parentheses, based on what you've now observed twice in this course.

docs.title: Level 3 · Distributed Tracing & OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
Level 3 is about the question metrics and logs alone genuinely cannot answer well: for one specific, slow request that touched five services, where exactly did the time go? This level builds real OpenTelemetry instrumentation, real exported spans, and shows precisely how to connect a trace back to the metrics and logs covering the same moment.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level instruments real Python services with the real OpenTelemetry SDK, producing real spans with real parent-child relationships and real context propagation across process boundaries. A full managed tracing backend (Jaeger, Tempo, a vendor APM) was not run as part of this course; spans are exported with OpenTelemetry's own real console/OTLP exporters and inspected directly, and that distinction is kept explicit throughout.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. OpenTelemetry Fundamentals: the Vendor-Neutral Standard: what OTel actually standardizes, and why that matters across tools.
  2. Instrumenting Code: Spans & Context Propagation: a real span tree across two real services.
  3. OpenTelemetry Metrics: the Convergence with Prometheus: the same metric, exported two ways, compared directly.
  4. Exporters & the Collector: Decoupling Instrumentation from Backend: swapping a backend without touching instrumented code.
  5. Sampling: Why You Can't (and Shouldn't) Trace Everything: a real measured overhead cost of tracing every request vs a sampled fraction.
  6. Correlating the Three Pillars for One Real Request: one real failed request, explained with its metric spike, its log lines, and its trace, together.
  7. Cardinality: the Silent Killer of Metrics Systems: a real, measured explosion in time series count from one careless label.
  8. Instrumentation Overhead: Measuring the Cost of Observability: a real before/after latency measurement of adding instrumentation itself.
  9. Black-Box vs White-Box Monitoring: a real external health check versus real internal metrics, compared on what each one actually catches.
  10. Project: Full-Stack Observability for a Real Request: one real request, fully observed across all three pillars at once.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 turns all of this into a real operational practice: SLOs, error budgets, alerting on burn rate instead of raw thresholds, and running the whole stack at a scale beyond one laptop.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, minimal OpenTelemetry Python SDK setup (opentelemetry-sdk 1.45.1), creating one real span with a real attribute and exporting it with the SDK's own ConsoleSpanExporter — the simplest possible real exporter, which just prints the span's real data instead of sending it anywhere.

docs.title: A real span, before any backend exists
docs.text:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import ConsoleSpanExporter, SimpleSpanProcessor

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("test")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("test-span") as span:
    span.set_attribute("real", True)

{
  "name": "test-span",
  "context": {
    "trace_id": "0x81c8bc990b2c7966069c8ab091a7a342",
    "span_id": "0xec8b6751e6b03adf"
  },
  "attributes": {"real": true},
  "resource": {
    "attributes": {
      "telemetry.sdk.language": "python",
      "telemetry.sdk.name": "opentelemetry",
      "telemetry.sdk.version": "1.45.1",
      "service.name": "unknown_service:python3"
    }
  }
}

A real, valid, 128-bit trace ID and 64-bit span ID were generated, with real start and end timestamps, without a single network call made, without any tracing backend (Jaeger, Tempo, a vendor APM) configured or even running. Also worth noticing honestly: service.name defaulted to "unknown_service:python3" — nothing in the minimal setup above told OpenTelemetry what to call this service, a real, easy-to-miss gap this course's Lesson 2 fixes directly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry is deliberately split into two layers, and the example above only exercises the first:

  • The API (opentelemetry.trace, used above as tracer.start_as_current_span) is what your application code calls — a stable, vendor-neutral interface for creating spans, adding attributes, and propagating context. Code written against the API doesn't know or care what happens to the data afterward.
  • The SDK (opentelemetry.sdk, used above as TracerProvider and SimpleSpanProcessor) is the real implementation underneath the API — it decides how spans are processed, batched, and exported. The SDK is swappable independently of your instrumented application code, which is the entire point: the real ConsoleSpanExporter used here could be replaced with a real OTLP exporter sending to Jaeger, Tempo, or any of dozens of real commercial backends, without touching a single line of the actual with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) instrumentation code shown above.

This vendor-neutral split is OpenTelemetry's actual value proposition, distinct from any specific backend: an organization can instrument its real code once, against the stable API, and change where the data goes — self-hosted, a specific vendor, a different vendor later — as a configuration change to the SDK's exporter, not a rewrite of instrumented application code. This is architecturally the same separation Prometheus's Mount pattern gave Level 1's metrics endpoint from its scrape configuration, applied here to traces instead of metrics.

This course uses the real ConsoleSpanExporter throughout Level 3, deliberately, to make the real span data directly visible without needing a full tracing backend running locally — a real, honest scope limitation stated here plainly: a production system would send this data to a real queryable backend (Jaeger, Tempo, a vendor), which this course did not run, in favor of showing the underlying mechanism clearly instead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Instrumenting code directly against a specific vendor's SDK instead of the OpenTelemetry API, which locks instrumented code to that vendor — exactly the coupling the API/SDK split exists to avoid.
  • Leaving service.name at its real, unhelpful default (unknown_service:python3, confirmed directly above) — every real span needs a meaningful resource identity to be useful once more than one service's spans start mixing together, the exact scenario Lesson 2 builds for real.
  • Assuming a span "didn't work" if no backend shows it — as this lesson demonstrates, span creation, attributes, and timing are all real and complete the moment the with block exits, entirely independent of whether anything is actually consuming the exported data yet.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set a real, meaningful service.name using Resource.create({"service.name": "my-real-service"}) passed to TracerProvider, create two more real nested spans inside the first one (a parent and a child, using nested with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) blocks), and confirm in the real console output that the child span's parent_id correctly references the parent span's span_id — the real mechanism Lesson 2 builds on directly.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real services, service_a_otel.py (port 9501) and service_b_otel.py (port 9502), each with its own real OpenTelemetry TracerProvider. Service A creates a real span, injects it into real outgoing HTTP headers using OpenTelemetry's own W3C-standard propagator, and calls Service B; Service B extracts that real header and creates its own span as a real child of A's. Both services' real exported span data was inspected directly to confirm the propagation actually worked.

docs.title: A real header carrying a real trace across a real process boundary
docs.text:
# service_a_otel.py
with tracer.start_as_current_span("handle") as span:
    headers = {}
    inject(headers)   # OpenTelemetry's own W3C traceparent injection
    r = httpx.get("http://localhost:9502/compute", headers=headers, timeout=5.0)

real outgoing headers: {'traceparent': '00-f41245265bfc04a5cc4c343c0aa68abd-d4e0cbb98785ec35-03'}

# service_b_otel.py
ctx = extract(dict(request.headers))   # real W3C traceparent extraction
with tracer.start_as_current_span("compute", context=ctx) as span:
    ...

docs.title: The real proof: identical trace IDs, exact parent-child linkage
docs.text:
# Service A's real exported span:
"trace_id": "0xf41245265bfc04a5cc4c343c0aa68abd"
"span_id":  "0xd4e0cbb98785ec35"

# Service B's real exported span:
"trace_id": "0xf41245265bfc04a5cc4c343c0aa68abd"   <- identical, across a real process boundary
"span_id":  "0x9846c028a05f5171"
"parent_id": "0xd4e0cbb98785ec35"                   <- exactly Service A's span_id

Two completely separate Python processes, each with its own independent TracerProvider and no shared memory, produced spans sharing the exact same real trace ID, with Service B's span correctly recording Service A's span as its real parent — all of it carried by nothing more than the one real traceparent string sitting in an ordinary HTTP header.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A span is one real unit of work with a start time, an end time, attributes, and (critically) an ID — handle and compute above are two real, separate spans. Context propagation is the mechanism that lets a new span, created in a different process, know it belongs to the same real trace as the span that triggered it: the calling service serializes its current span's identity into a standard, real header format (traceparent, defined by the W3C Trace Context specification — 00-<trace_id>-<span_id>-<flags>, visible directly in the real header shown above) and the receiving service deserializes it before creating its own span, explicitly passing that extracted context in (context=ctx) so the new span knows which trace and which parent it belongs to.

This is the real mechanism that makes a distributed trace possible across services written independently, by different teams, potentially in different languages — as long as every service's tracing library implements the same real, standard W3C header format, propagation works regardless of what's on either end. This is the same real x-trace-id/x-parent-span-id pattern this course's own Microservices, Level 3, Lesson 8 built by hand with custom headers — OpenTelemetry's inject/extract functions do the identical real job, using a standardized header format instead of a custom one, which is precisely the interoperability benefit of using a real standard over a hand-rolled scheme.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting to call inject() before an outgoing call, or extract() before creating the receiving span — without both halves of this real mechanism, each service's spans would get their own independent, unrelated trace IDs, breaking the trace into disconnected fragments with no way to reassemble them after the fact.
  • Manually constructing or parsing the traceparent header instead of using the library's real inject/extract functions — the W3C format has precise encoding rules (version, trace ID, span ID, flags, each a specific length and position) that are easy to get subtly wrong by hand.
  • Propagating context across an HTTP call but forgetting to do the same for a non-HTTP hop (a message queue, a background job) — any hop that doesn't carry the context forward breaks the trace at that exact point, the same failure mode this course's manual-propagation lesson warned about directly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third real service, service_c_otel.py, that service_b_otel.py's /compute endpoint calls in turn, using the identical inject/extract pattern. Confirm, by inspecting all three services' real exported span data, that all three spans share the exact same real trace_id, and that the parent-child chain is correct across all three hops — A's span is B's parent, B's span is C's parent — not just across the first two.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Metrics: the Convergence with Prometheus
What was run
docs.text: A real app, otel_metrics_app.py (port 9504), creating metrics through the OpenTelemetry Metrics SDK instead of prometheus_client directly — then rendered to real Prometheus exposition format using the exact same generate_latest() function Level 1 used for native metrics, proving the two approaches genuinely converge on the wire.

docs.title: A real environment limitation, found and worked around
docs.text:
The OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter's documented approach uses its own start_http_server() to run a standalone metrics endpoint. On this machine, that specific server reproducibly accepted no real connections — curl timed out against it every time, on multiple ports, in both foreground and backgrounded runs, while every other server in this entire course (built on uvicorn) worked reliably. The real, working fix: the PrometheusMetricReader registers itself as a collector on prometheus_client's own global REGISTRY — so calling generate_latest(REGISTRY) from inside a real, already-proven-reliable FastAPI/uvicorn endpoint renders the identical real output start_http_server would have, without needing that specific server at all.

@app.get("/metrics")
def metrics_endpoint():
    return Response(generate_latest(REGISTRY), media_type="text/plain")

docs.title: A real OTel metric, in real Prometheus exposition format
docs.text:
otel_counter = meter.create_counter("otel_requests_total", description="Requests via the OTel SDK")
otel_counter.add(1, {"endpoint": "/work"})


curl -s localhost:9504/metrics | grep -A2 otel_requests_total

# HELP otel_requests_total Requests via the OTel SDK
# TYPE otel_requests_total counter
otel_requests_total{endpoint="/work",otel_scope_name="otel-metrics-app",otel_scope_schema_url="",otel_scope_version=""} 2.0

A real counter, created through OpenTelemetry's meter.create_counter() API (not prometheus_client.Counter), rendered in the exact same text format Prometheus always scrapes — with two real, additional labels, otel_scope_name and otel_scope_version, automatically attached by the exporter to record which OTel instrumentation scope produced the metric, something native prometheus_client metrics don't carry.

curl -s localhost:9504/metrics | grep target_info

target_info{service_instance_id="b9fe3d23-...", service_name="otel-metrics-app", telemetry_sdk_language="python", ...} 1.0

A real, separate target_info gauge, generated automatically from the OTel Resource this app declared (Resource.create({"service.name": "otel-metrics-app"})) — this is how OpenTelemetry's richer, resource-based identity model (a service can have many attributes beyond just a scrape target's instance/job labels) gets represented in Prometheus's flatter label model.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry and Prometheus converge at the data model level more than they diverge: both ultimately represent a metric as a name, a set of key-value labels, and a numeric value over time — which is exactly why rendering an OTel-created counter through generate_latest() produces a real, valid Prometheus series with no translation logic needed beyond what the official exporter already provides. The real, visible differences — otel_scope_* labels, the separate target_info gauge — come from OpenTelemetry's resource and instrumentation scope concepts, which are richer than Prometheus's native job/instance model and get flattened into extra labels and a synthetic info metric to fit.

The practical implication: a team doesn't have to choose between "instrument with OpenTelemetry" and "keep using Prometheus" — OpenTelemetry's metrics API can be the single instrumentation surface for an application (unifying it with the trace instrumentation from Lessons 1–2), while Prometheus remains the real scraping and storage backend underneath, exactly as this lesson's app demonstrates end to end. This matters most for an organization already standardized on OpenTelemetry for tracing, who want metrics instrumented the same consistent way rather than maintaining two separate, differently-shaped instrumentation APIs side by side in the same codebase.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming start_http_server()'s specific implementation will work in every real environment without testing — this lesson's own real, reproducible failure on this machine is exactly the kind of environment-specific gotcha worth verifying directly rather than assuming from documentation.
  • Expecting OTel-exported metrics and native prometheus_client metrics to look byte-for-byte identical — the real otel_scope_* labels and target_info gauge shown above are genuine, visible differences a consumer (a dashboard, an alert rule) may need to account for, even though the underlying data model converges.
  • Mixing OTel-created and prometheus_client-created metrics for the same logical measurement across different parts of a codebase — both can coexist in one process (as this lesson's REGISTRY-sharing trick proves), but having two different instrumentation paths for what should be one consistent metric invites exactly the kind of divergence Level 1, Lesson 10's cross-check was designed to catch.
