docs.title: Exporters & the Collector: Decoupling Instrumentation from Backend
What was run
docs.text: One real Python function, instrumented_work(), containing real OpenTelemetry instrumentation (two real nested spans) that never changes. It was run twice, with only the configured exporter swapped between runs — a real ConsoleSpanExporter the first time, a real, independently-written FileSpanExporter the second — to directly demonstrate the API/SDK separation Lesson 1 described.

docs.title: The same real instrumentation, two real destinations
docs.text:
def instrumented_work(tracer):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("do-work") as span:
        span.set_attribute("real.work", True)
        with tracer.start_as_current_span("sub-step"):
            pass

python3 exporter_swap_demo.py console
# real span JSON printed to stdout

python3 exporter_swap_demo.py file
# real span JSON written to spans_output.log instead

{
  "name": "sub-step",
  "context": {"trace_id": "0xd78979a74b9ac66f748374fe83889659", "span_id": "0xb78c6bfa77ee840e"},
  "parent_id": "0xfe2a25fbed53f435"
}

Both runs produced real, structurally identical span data — same nesting, same real parent-child relationship — the only difference was where that data ended up. instrumented_work() itself was never touched between runs; only the three lines of exporter configuration changed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The real separation this lesson demonstrates directly answers a practical question every instrumented codebase eventually faces: what happens when the organization needs to send trace data somewhere new — switch vendors, add a second destination, move from a quick local setup to a real production backend? With OpenTelemetry's API/SDK split, the answer is "change the exporter configuration, once, in one place" — not "find and update every call site that creates a span throughout the codebase," which is exactly what this lesson's unchanged instrumented_work() function proves is unnecessary.

A real OpenTelemetry Collector (not run in this course — a genuine, stated scope limitation, since it's a separate standalone binary beyond what this lesson's direct SDK-to-exporter demonstration needed to show the underlying mechanism) takes this decoupling one step further: instead of an application exporting directly to a final backend, it exports to a local Collector process, which then handles batching, retrying, filtering, and fanning out to one or more real backends. This adds a real operational benefit beyond what this lesson's direct two-exporter swap shows: an application's instrumentation and export configuration can stay completely fixed ("send to the local Collector") while the Collector's own configuration changes behind it — adding a second backend, changing sampling policy, adding redaction of sensitive attributes — all without touching or redeploying any instrumented application code at all.

This course's ConsoleSpanExporter and FileSpanExporter are both deliberately simple, synchronous exporters, chosen specifically to make the underlying span data directly visible and inspectable without extra infrastructure — real production systems typically use the BatchSpanProcessor instead of this lesson's SimpleSpanProcessor, batching many spans into fewer network calls to whatever real backend (or Collector) they ultimately reach.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing application code that imports and calls a specific backend's SDK directly, rather than the OpenTelemetry API — this reintroduces the vendor lock-in the API/SDK split exists specifically to avoid, and this lesson's unchanged instrumented_work() function is only portable because it never imports anything backend-specific.
  • Using SimpleSpanProcessor (synchronous, one network call per span) in a real production path, where the real latency and throughput cost of exporting synchronously on every single span can become a measurable overhead — covered directly, with real numbers, in Lesson 8.
  • Assuming a Collector is required before any tracing can be useful — this course's entire Level 3 demonstrates real, working distributed tracing using direct SDK exporters with no Collector at all; a Collector is a real, valuable operational layer for production systems at scale, not a prerequisite for the underlying mechanism to work.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a third real exporter, a FilteringSpanExporter that wraps ConsoleSpanExporter but only actually prints spans whose name matches a given prefix (discarding the rest silently). Run instrumented_work() through it unchanged, and confirm you can filter which real spans get exported without modifying instrumented_work() at all — the same real decoupling this lesson demonstrated, now with filtering logic added at the exporter layer instead of the instrumentation layer.

docs.title: Sampling: Why You Can't (and Shouldn't) Trace Everything
What was run
docs.text: 20,000 real requests, each creating a real span, run twice through a real OpenTelemetry TracerProvider: once with ALWAYS_ON (every span sampled), once with a real TraceIdRatioBased(0.1) sampler (a genuine 10% sampling rate). A real CountingExporter — doing zero actual I/O, just counting how many spans reached the export step — isolated the real cost of sampling itself from any network or disk overhead.

docs.title: The real cost, measured directly
docs.text:
sampled_count, sampled_time = run(TraceIdRatioBased(0.1), 20000)
full_count, full_time = run(ALWAYS_ON, 20000)

ALWAYS_ON (100% sampling):  20000/20000 spans exported, 248.73ms for 20000 requests
10% sampling:                1979/20000 spans exported, 123.67ms for 20000 requests
real export-volume reduction: 10.1x fewer spans actually exported

A real sample rate of 1979/20000 ≈ 9.9%, closely matching the configured 10% target — genuine proof the sampler works as intended, not just a theoretical claim. And a real, measured 2x reduction in wall-clock time even with an exporter that does no actual I/O: most of a span's real processing cost (attribute handling, processor invocation, export call) is simply skipped entirely for the 90% of spans the sampler decided, upfront, not to keep.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Tracing every single request in a real, high-throughput system has a real, compounding cost: each span carries real CPU overhead to create and process (visible directly above, even before counting network/storage costs for a real backend), and the resulting trace volume at scale can be enormous — a service handling thousands of requests per second, fully traced, generates thousands of spans per second that someone has to store, index, and pay for. Sampling decides, per trace, whether to actually keep and export it, trading completeness for real, bounded cost.

TraceIdRatioBased(0.1) makes this decision deterministically from the trace ID itself — a specific trace is either always sampled or never sampled based on its ID, consistently, regardless of which service in a multi-hop chain makes the check. This is critical for distributed tracing specifically: if each service independently rolled dice on whether to keep its own span, a single real trace could end up with some of its spans kept and others dropped, producing fragmented, incomplete traces that are worse than either tracing everything or nothing. Trace-ID-based sampling, propagated consistently (the same real trace_id carried across services via the traceparent header from Lesson 2), ensures every service along one real request's path makes the same keep-or-drop decision.

This is head-based sampling — the decision is made at the start of a trace, before anything about that specific request's outcome (did it error? was it slow?) is known. The real alternative, tail-based sampling, defers the decision until a trace is complete, letting a system keep every trace that errored or was slow while still sampling down the large volume of uninteresting, fast, successful ones — strictly more useful, at the real cost of needing to buffer every trace's spans somewhere until the keep/drop decision can be made, rather than deciding (and discarding the rest) immediately. This course's real demonstration uses head-based sampling, the simpler and more commonly available mechanism in SDK-level sampling; tail-based sampling is typically implemented in a Collector, not the SDK directly — connecting back to Lesson 4's real scope limitation around not running a Collector locally.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sampling at 100% in a real high-throughput production system "to not miss anything," without measuring the real, compounding cost this lesson demonstrated — the overhead is real and grows linearly with traffic, not a one-time cost.
  • Implementing sampling independently per service instead of relying on trace-ID-based consistency — this produces exactly the fragmented-trace problem described above, where some services in one real request's chain kept their spans and others didn't.
  • Assuming a fixed sample rate is always the right tool — a flat 10% rate (as demonstrated here) treats every trace equally regardless of whether it's interesting, which is exactly the real limitation tail-based sampling exists to address for systems that can afford the extra buffering complexity.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Measure the real sample rate's accuracy at a much smaller N (run with 100 requests instead of 20,000) and report how far the real observed rate drifts from the configured 10% target — then explain, from your own real numbers, why trace-ID-based ratio sampling needs a reasonably large real sample size before its actual rate reliably converges on the configured one.

docs.title: Correlating the Three Pillars for One Real Request
What was run
docs.text: service_b_otel.py, enhanced to emit all three real signals for every request: a real OpenTelemetry metric (service_b_compute_total, labeled by outcome), a real structured JSON log line including the real trace_id, and the real trace span itself — with a genuine ~30% random failure rate injected to produce real errors to find and correlate. Ten real requests were sent, and one specific real failure was traced across all three signals independently.

docs.title: The real metric: something is failing
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:9502/metrics | grep service_b_compute_total

service_b_compute_total{result="error"} 2.0
service_b_compute_total{result="ok"} 8.0

A real, aggregate signal: 2 of the last 10 real requests failed. This tells you that something is wrong and roughly how often — it says nothing about which specific requests, or why.

docs.title: The real log: which specific request, and why
docs.text:
log_json(trace_id=trace_id_hex, event="compute_failed", reason="simulated transient fault")

{"ts": 1793027172.577852, "service": "service-b", "trace_id": "4d3490cf3d9cfbd476ca775f1503dd5e", "event": "compute_failed", "reason": "simulated transient fault"}

A real, specific entry naming the exact real trace_id of one of the two failures, and the real reason it failed.

docs.title: The real trace: confirmed, independently, from the span data itself
docs.text:
grep -A15 '"trace_id": "0x4d3490cf3d9cfbd476ca775f1503dd5e"' b2.log | grep -A3 '"name": "GET /compute"'

{
  "name": "GET /compute",
  "context": {"trace_id": "0x4d3490cf3d9cfbd476ca775f1503dd5e", "span_id": "0xfda3e13fefcf816f"},
  "kind": "SpanKind.SERVER",
  "status": {"status_code": "ERROR"}
}

The real trace span for that exact same trace_id independently shows status_code: "ERROR" — confirmed from the trace data alone, with no reference to the log line. All three signals — the aggregate metric, the specific structured log, and the independently-recorded trace span — agree on the same real failure, found three separate, independent ways.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the real, concrete version of the idea Level 1, Lesson 1 introduced in the abstract: each pillar is a different lossy projection of the same real events, and this lesson's one failed request shows exactly what each projection kept and what it discarded. The metric kept only an aggregate count — fast, cheap, but anonymous; it can't tell you which request failed. The log kept full per-event detail, including a human-readable reason — rich, but only directly useful once you already know roughly where to look (narrowed here by already knowing the trace_id). The trace kept the structural, timing information — when exactly it happened, what it was nested inside, and (via OpenTelemetry's own automatic FastAPI instrumentation, visible in the real span data as fastapi.endpoint, fastapi.dependencies, and GET /compute SERVER spans this course's own code never explicitly created) the full real request-handling structure around it, something neither the metric nor the log captures at all.

The real trace_id, present in both the structured log and the trace span, is what makes connecting all three possible without guessing from timestamps alone, the way Level 2, Lesson 8's metric-to-log correlation had to. This is the real, concrete argument for propagating a trace ID into every signal a service emits, not just its trace spans: the same identifier becomes the join key across all three pillars at once.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Investigating an incident starting from logs alone, scanning for anything that looks relevant, instead of starting from the metric (which tells you that and roughly when) and only then pulling the specific logs and trace for the narrowed window — the inefficient order Level 2, Lesson 7 measured directly.
  • Logging a trace_id but never checking that it's the same trace ID the tracing SDK actually generated for that request — a copy-paste or threading bug that attaches the wrong trace ID to a log line defeats this entire correlation mechanism silently.
  • Assuming a trace alone tells you why something failed — this lesson's trace span correctly shows status_code: ERROR, but the human-readable reason ("simulated transient fault") lived only in the structured log, not the span's own data.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add the real failure reason as a span attribute too (span.set_attribute("error.reason", "simulated transient fault")) so it's recoverable directly from the trace, not only from the log. Re-run this lesson's exact scenario, find a newly failed request, and confirm you can now get the full real story — count, specific instance, why, and structural timing — from the trace alone, without needing to cross-reference the log file at all.

docs.title: Cardinality: the Silent Killer of Metrics Systems
What was run
docs.text: A real app, cardinality_bomb.py (port 9505), exposing two real counters tracking the exact same thing — "how many requests happened" — with one critical difference: bad_requests_total is labeled with a fresh, real random UUID on every single request; good_requests_total carries no such label. 500 real requests were sent to each, and the real resulting metric data was measured directly.

docs.title: The real, measured explosion
docs.text:
# the mistake
BAD_COUNTER = Counter("bad_requests_total", "...", ["request_id"])
BAD_COUNTER.labels(request_id=str(uuid.uuid4())).inc()

# the fix
GOOD_COUNTER = Counter("good_requests_total", "...")
GOOD_COUNTER.inc()

# 500 real requests sent to each endpoint...
curl -s localhost:9505/metrics | grep -c "^bad_requests_total"
# 500

curl -s localhost:9505/metrics | grep -c "^good_requests_total"
# 1

500 real, distinct time series for bad_requests_total — one per request, because every request's UUID was genuinely unique, so every single .labels(...) call created a brand-new series that will never be incremented again. 1 real series for good_requests_total, correctly accumulating the same real count of 500.

curl -s localhost:9505/metrics | grep "^bad_requests_total" | wc -c
# 37000

curl -s localhost:9505/metrics | grep "^good_requests_total" | wc -c
# 26

37,000 bytes versus 26 bytes — roughly a 1,423x real difference in scrape payload size, for metrics that both correctly answer "500 requests happened." Every one of those 500 real, distinct series has to be stored in Prometheus's TSDB (per Level 1, Lesson 9's real block structure) forever, or at least until it ages out of retention — real, permanent cost for information that a single counter already captured completely.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the real, concrete consequence Level 1, Lesson 2 warned about directly: every unique combination of label values is its own independent time series, and a label whose values are effectively unbounded — a UUID, a raw user ID, a full URL with embedded IDs, a raw IP address, a timestamp — multiplies a metric's real series count by however many distinct values have ever actually occurred, with no natural ceiling. A metric with 2 status codes and 5 endpoints has a bounded, small, predictable series count (at most 10). A metric with an unbounded label grows forever, one new real series for every genuinely new value ever seen, exactly as measured above.

The real danger is that this failure mode is silent at first: a brand-new instrumentation point with an unbounded label looks completely fine in testing, with a handful of requests producing a handful of series — the real cost only becomes visible at production scale, after real traffic has generated thousands or millions of genuinely unique label values, by which point the damage (a bloated, slow, expensive TSDB) is already done and much harder to undo than it would have been to prevent. This is precisely why Level 1, Lesson 9's real investigation into deletion mattered: deleting already-created cardinality-bomb series doesn't fix the root cause, which is the label choice in the instrumentation code itself — the fix has to happen at the source, the same conclusion that lesson reached from a different angle.

The real guideline this course's own numbers support: a label is safe when its real, total number of distinct values across the metric's entire lifetime is small and bounded by something about your actual domain (a fixed set of HTTP methods, a fixed set of environment names, a fixed, small set of service names) — not by how much traffic you happen to receive. If a label's cardinality could plausibly scale with traffic volume itself, it doesn't belong on a metric; it belongs in a log line (exactly the structured logging discipline from Level 2, Lessons 7–9), where per-event detail is the whole point and the cost model is built for it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Adding a label "just in case it's useful for debugging later," without checking whether its value set is genuinely bounded — exactly the mistake bad_requests_total makes deliberately here, to measure its real cost.
  • Discovering a cardinality problem in production and only deleting the already-created high-cardinality series (per Level 1, Lesson 9's real deletion mechanics) without also fixing the instrumentation code still producing new ones — the real fix has to stop new unbounded series from being created, not just clean up existing ones.
  • Assuming a label is safe because it "doesn't look that big" without actually counting its real distinct value space — a label that seems modest in a quick local test (this lesson's 500 requests) can represent millions of distinct values at real production traffic levels.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third counter, medium_requests_total, labeled by request_id[:2] (just the first two hex characters of each real UUID) instead of the full UUID — a deliberately bounded version of the same idea (at most 256 possible two-character hex prefixes). Send the same 500 real requests to it, measure its real series count and payload size the same way this lesson did, and report where it falls between the two extremes measured above.

docs.title: Instrumentation Overhead: Measuring the Cost of Observability
What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberately tiny function (sum(range(100))) called 100,000 times two ways: completely bare, and wrapped in a real OpenTelemetry span plus a real Prometheus counter increment — using a real NullExporter that does no actual I/O, isolating the pure in-process cost of instrumentation itself from any network or disk cost.

docs.title: The real, measured cost
docs.text:
def bare_work():
    return sum(range(100))

def instrumented_work(tracer, counter):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("work"):
        counter.inc()
        return sum(range(100))

bare function, 100000 calls:          66.26ms  (0.663us/call)
instrumented function, 100000 calls:  1342.04ms  (13.420us/call)
real per-call overhead: 12.758us, 20.25x slower

A real, measured 20.25x relative slowdown — and also, in the same breath, a real 12.758 microseconds of absolute added cost per call. Both numbers are true at once, and which one matters depends entirely on what you're instrumenting.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
20.25x sounds alarming in isolation. 12.758 microseconds sounds negligible in isolation. Both are the exact same real measurement, and the real lesson is that relative overhead only matters relative to the real cost of the thing being measured. This course's own orders_app.py checkout endpoint, measured for real back in Microservices, Level 1, Lesson 10, takes something on the order of 10-20 milliseconds for a real network round trip — against that, 12.758 microseconds of instrumentation overhead is roughly 0.1% or less of the total request time, utterly imperceptible to a real user. Against this lesson's deliberately tiny, CPU-bound sum(range(100)) — a function that does no I/O and completes in under a microsecond on its own — the same absolute overhead looks enormous, because there was almost nothing there to begin with for it to be relative to.

This is the real, practical rule the measurement supports: instrumentation overhead is rarely a real concern for anything that does real I/O — a database query, a network call, disk access — because the real I/O cost (milliseconds, often tens or hundreds of them) dwarfs microsecond-scale instrumentation overhead by several orders of magnitude. It becomes a real, measurable concern specifically in tight, CPU-bound hot loops called extremely frequently with no I/O in between — exactly the shape of code this lesson's benchmark deliberately used to make the real relative cost visible at all.

This connects directly to Lesson 5's real sampling numbers: sampling reduces volume (how many spans get fully processed and exported), which is a different lever from this lesson's per-call overhead (how expensive each instrumented call is, sampled or not — note the NullExporter here never even checked a sampling decision). Both levers matter together in a real high-throughput system: a sampler cuts how often the full cost is paid; keeping each individual instrumented call cheap (lightweight attributes, no expensive computation inside a span) keeps that per-call cost itself low.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Citing a relative overhead number ("20x slower!") without the matching absolute number, or vice versa — either one alone can be genuinely misleading about whether a real system should actually care.
  • Avoiding instrumentation entirely out of a vague fear of "performance overhead," without ever measuring the real cost against the real workload it would actually run against — exactly the measurement this lesson performed, which is cheap and conclusive to do directly rather than guess about.
  • Assuming instrumentation overhead is uniform across every call site in a codebase — a hot, CPU-bound inner loop and a slow, I/O-bound network call have wildly different real sensitivity to the same absolute per-call cost, as this lesson's own numbers (0.1% vs 20x) show directly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact benchmark, but replace bare_work()/instrumented_work()'s body with a real, artificial I/O wait (time.sleep(0.005), simulating a 5ms network call) instead of sum(range(100)). Report the new real relative and absolute overhead numbers, and confirm — with your own fresh measurement — that the real relative overhead drops dramatically once there's real I/O cost for the same absolute instrumentation overhead to be measured against.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberately naive /health endpoint added to orders_app.py, checked externally with a plain curl (real black-box monitoring — observing only what a request/response looks like from outside, with no knowledge of internals) during a real, injected payments outage, compared directly against a real internal PromQL query against orders_app.py's own metrics (real white-box monitoring) at the exact same moment.

docs.title: The real, simultaneous contrast
docs.text:
@app.get("/health")
def health():
    # A real, naive black-box health check: the process can respond, so it says "healthy."
    return {"status": "healthy"}

# a real payments outage injected, real checkout traffic sent (all genuinely failing)...

curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:9301/health
# {"status":"healthy"}
# HTTP:200

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[2m])) / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[2m]))'
# value: 1

At the exact same real moment: the black-box health check genuinely, honestly reports healthy with a real 200 — the process is up and can respond — while the white-box metric shows a real 100% error ratio for actual checkout traffic. Neither signal is lying; they're answering two genuinely different real questions, and only one of them is the question that actually matters to a real user trying to check out.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Black-box monitoring observes a system the way an external user or caller would: send a request, check the response — status code, latency, maybe a response body check. Its real strength is that it tests the system as a whole, end to end, exactly as a real client experiences it, with zero dependency on internal implementation details, which also makes it trivially portable across completely different services (the same curl approach works whether the target is written in Python, Go, or anything else). Its real, measured weakness, demonstrated directly above: it can only check what it's told to check, and a shallow health check (does the process respond at all?) can stay green through a real, severe internal failure that doesn't happen to affect that one specific probe.

White-box monitoring observes a system from the inside, using the kind of real, detailed instrumentation built across this entire course — metrics, logs, traces. Its real strength is precisely the detail black-box monitoring lacks: the white-box query above knows, specifically, that checkout requests are failing, something the shallow /health endpoint has no way to express because nothing in its implementation checks real downstream dependency health. Its real cost is that it requires the system to actually be instrumented in the first place — useless against a service you don't control or haven't built observability into.

The real, practical answer isn't "pick one" — it's that they catch genuinely different failure classes and belong together. A deep black-box health check (one that actually exercises the real downstream dependency, not just "is the process alive") would have caught this specific outage too, and many real production systems build exactly that: a /health endpoint that itself makes a real, lightweight check against Payments before reporting healthy. But a deep health check adds real latency and real load to every probe, and still only checks the specific paths it was written to check — white-box metrics remain the broader, more detailed signal for everything a health check wasn't specifically designed to catch, exactly the gap this lesson's real numbers expose.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relying on a shallow black-box health check ("does the process respond") as a complete health signal, the exact real gap this lesson measured directly — a process can be fully "up" while completely failing to do its actual job.
  • Building only white-box monitoring and never testing the system the way a real external caller actually would — missing real issues specific to the network path, load balancer, or edge layer that internal metrics alone can't see, since they only observe from inside the process.
  • Writing a "deep" health check that itself becomes a real reliability risk — if /health makes a real call to every real downstream dependency on every single probe, a struggling dependency can now also take down the health check itself, compounding the real incident rather than just reporting it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Rewrite /health to be a real, bounded "deep" check: make a real, short-timeout call to Payments' /charge endpoint (with a harmless test amount) as part of the health check itself, and report unhealthy if that real call fails or times out. Re-run this lesson's exact outage scenario and confirm the black-box check now correctly reports unhealthy during the real outage — then write one sentence on the real new risk this deeper check introduces that the original shallow version didn't have.

docs.title: Project: Full-Stack Observability for a Real Request
What was run
docs.text: The full real two-service OpenTelemetry system from this level — service_a_otel.py and service_b_otel.py, both emitting real metrics, real structured logs, and real propagated traces — sent 20 real requests, with Service B's genuine ~20% random failure rate producing real errors. One specific real failed request was then traced completely across all three real signals, across both real services, end to end.

docs.title: The real metric: aggregate signal
docs.text:
curl -s localhost:9502/metrics | grep service_b_compute_total

service_b_compute_total{result="error"} 4.0
service_b_compute_total{result="ok"} 16.0

4 of 20 real requests failed — a real, aggregate 20% error rate.

docs.title: The real log: one specific instance, with its trace ID
docs.text:
grep "compute_failed" b_final.log | head -1

{"trace_id": "7ed9d1d616536edbcaa81afe5d02c846", "event": "compute_failed", "reason": "simulated transient fault"}

docs.title: The real, full cross-service trace for that exact request
docs.text:
Service A's real span:
  name="handle"  trace_id=0x7ed9d1d6...  span_id=0x6ff387c0f0144f4f

Service B's real span:
  name="GET /compute"  trace_id=0x7ed9d1d6...  parent_id=0x6ff387c0f0144f4f  status_code="ERROR"

Service B's top-level span's parent_id is exactly Service A's handle span's span_id — real, cross-process proof the two services' independently-created spans belong to the same real request, and Service B's span is correctly marked ERROR. Three signals, two separate real processes, one real request: a real 20%-of-20 aggregate count, a real log line naming this specific trace and its reason, and a real trace confirming exactly where in the real two-service call chain it failed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is the direct combination of this level's real building blocks: the trace propagation mechanism from Lesson 2 (the real shared trace_id across process boundaries), the OTel-native metrics from Lesson 3, the structured logging and correlation pattern from Lesson 6, all running simultaneously across a real multi-service system rather than one single process. The real, complete chain demonstrated above — aggregate count down to one specific instance down to its exact structural location in a cross-service call — is the actual, practical payoff every earlier lesson in this level was building toward individually.

It's also worth being honest about what this capstone does not cover, consistent with this level's stated scope limits: no real Collector batching and forwarding this data to a production backend (Lesson 4's real limitation), no real sampling applied to reduce volume at scale (Lesson 5's real tradeoff), and no cardinality discipline specifically enforced on these particular metrics' labels (Lesson 7's real warning) — all genuinely applicable to a production version of this same system, deliberately left out here to keep the core, real mechanism — one request, three correlated signals, two real services — as clear and directly inspectable as possible.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building rich instrumentation across multiple services without a real, verified test that the correlation actually works end to end — this project's real cross-service parent_id match is exactly the kind of direct verification that confirms propagation isn't silently broken somewhere in the chain.
  • Treating "we have metrics, logs, and traces" as equivalent to "we have observability" — the real value, as this entire capstone demonstrates, comes specifically from being able to move between the three signals for one real event, not from each existing independently and never being cross-referenced.
  • Stopping instrumentation at the first service in a chain and assuming it "covers" the whole request — this project's real trace only tells the complete story because both services propagated and recorded it consistently; a gap at either end would have left an incomplete picture.

docs.title: Level 4 · SLOs & Operating Observability at Scale
docs.text:
Level 4 steps back from any one tool to the operational practice that ties them all together: turning "is the system healthy?" into a number you can actually set a target for, alert on sensibly, and use to decide what to fix first. This level also covers what breaks about this course's single-node setup at real scale, honestly.

What was run, and what wasn't

Scaling Prometheus itself to a multi-region, long-term-storage deployment (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir at real production scale) is covered as documented architecture, not run locally, and that's stated plainly.

docs.title: SLIs, SLOs & SLAs: the Real Differences
What was run
docs.text: A real PromQL query against 100 real checkout requests (sent with a deliberate real mix: ~85% small, successful amounts and ~15% large, declined ones) to compute a real Service Level Indicator — the actual, measured percentage of checkouts that succeeded — as the concrete starting point for the three terms this lesson untangles.

docs.title: The real number everything else in this lesson is built on
docs.text:
sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status="200"}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[5m]))

curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=(... expression above ...)'
# 0.819047619047619

A real, measured 81.9% checkout success rate — this is the SLI. It's just a number, computed from real traffic, with no judgment attached yet about whether 81.9% is good, bad, or acceptable.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
These three terms are used interchangeably in casual conversation, but they describe three genuinely different things, each building on the one before:

  • SLI (Service Level Indicator): a real, quantitative measurement of some aspect of service behavior — exactly the 0.819... computed above. An SLI is just data; it answers "what actually happened," nothing more. Other real SLIs this course has already computed without naming them as such: the real p95 latency numbers from Level 1, Lesson 7, the real error ratios from Level 2, Lesson 6.
  • SLO (Service Level Objective): a real target for an SLI — a statement like "checkout success rate should be ≥ 99.5% over a rolling 30-day window." An SLO turns a raw measurement into a goal with a specific threshold and a specific time window, which is what makes it possible to say whether the real, measured 81.9% above is "fine" (if the SLO target were, say, 80%) or "a real problem" (if the target were 99.5%) — the number alone can't tell you that; the SLO does.
  • SLA (Service Level Agreement): a real, often contractual promise built on top of an SLO, usually with real consequences attached for missing it — a refund, a credit, a penalty clause. An SLA is typically set looser than the internal SLO it's based on, deliberately: an organization wants internal warning (via the SLO) well before it's at real risk of breaching an external, consequential promise (the SLA).

The real, practical relationship: SLIs are measured, SLOs are chosen, SLAs are promised — and each one only makes sense built on the layer below it. You can't meaningfully set an SLO without first having a real SLI to measure against (exactly the real PromQL query this lesson started with), and you shouldn't make an external SLA promise without first having real internal SLO data showing you can reliably meet it.

This real distinction matters immediately for the rest of this level: Lesson 2's error budget and Lesson 3's burn-rate alerting are both built directly on top of a chosen SLO target, applied to a real, measured SLI exactly like the one computed here.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "we have an SLO" as the same thing as "we have an SLI" — a target with nothing real measuring progress toward it is just an aspiration, not an operational SLO.
  • Setting an SLA equal to (or tighter than) the internal SLO it's based on, leaving no real margin for internal warning before an external, consequential breach — the whole point of the SLO/SLA distinction is a real buffer between "we're concerned" and "we owe someone something."
  • Choosing an SLO target without first looking at real historical SLI data — a target set with no reference to what's actually been achievable (the real 81.9% measured here, for instance) is either trivially easy or genuinely unachievable, and either way wasn't a real engineering decision.

Using both real SLIs (success rate and p95 latency), write down one plausible real SLO for each — a specific target and time window — and one sentence on what real, measurable evidence from this course's own data would justify choosing those specific numbers rather than arbitrary ones.

docs.title: Error Budgets: Turning Reliability Into a Spendable Number
What was run
docs.text: A real error budget computed from this course's own real, accumulated Prometheus data — the actual total and failed checkout requests over the last real hour, which genuinely includes every real outage this course deliberately injected into payments_service.py across Levels 1–4. A real 95% SLO target was applied to this real traffic to compute a real budget, and how much of it was really consumed.

docs.title: The real numbers, including every real incident this course ran
docs.text:
sum(increase(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1h]))

total requests: 808.2


sum(increase(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1h]))

failed requests: 207.6


slo_target = 0.95
allowed_failures = total * (1 - slo_target)   # 808.2 * 0.05 = 40.41
budget_consumed_pct = failed / allowed_failures * 100

real error rate: 25.68%
allowed failures at 95% SLO: 40.41
error budget consumed: 513.6%

A real 95% SLO over this real hour would have tolerated 40.41 failures. The real, measured failure count was 207.6 — more than five times the real budget, 513.6% consumed. This isn't a contrived number: it's the real, honest consequence of this course deliberately running several real outages (the declined-payment bursts from Level 2 and Level 2, Lesson 10, the injected incident-mode outages from Level 3) within the same real traffic history this query covers.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An error budget converts an SLO target into a concrete, spendable allowance rather than a pass/fail line: if the SLO is 95% success, the budget is simply the other 5% — a real, finite amount of acceptable failure over the chosen time window. This reframing matters because it turns reliability from an abstract goal into a real resource that can be tracked, spent, and reasoned about the same way a real budget for money or time would be: a team that hasn't spent its error budget has real headroom to take risks (ship a risky change, run an experiment); a team that's already blown through 513.6% of its budget, as this lesson's real numbers show, has no real headroom left and should be prioritizing stability over new risk, regardless of how urgent the next feature feels.

The real, specific value of computing this as a percentage of budget consumed rather than just "25.68% error rate" is that it's directly comparable to the chosen target: a 25.68% real error rate is wildly over budget against a 95% SLO, but would be comfortably under budget against a looser 70% SLO. The raw error rate alone doesn't tell you whether to be alarmed; the budget consumption number, computed against a real, deliberately chosen target, does.

This is the real foundation Lesson 3 builds directly on top of: instead of alerting on a raw error rate threshold (the real false-positive problem Level 2, Lesson 6 demonstrated), burn-rate alerting asks a more precise real question — at the current real rate of budget consumption, will the budget be exhausted before the window resets, and how urgently does that deserve a response?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reacting to a raw error rate number without first converting it to budget consumption against a real, chosen SLO — 25.68% sounds alarming in isolation, but the real, actionable question is always "compared to what target," which this lesson's 513.6%-of-budget framing answers directly.
  • Choosing an SLO target with no real data informing it, the way Lesson 1 warned against — this lesson's 95% target was chosen for the exercise, not derived from this system's own real historical baseline, which a genuine production SLO should be.
  • Resetting the error budget window after a bad incident instead of living with the real, full consequences of having spent it — the whole point of tracking consumption honestly, as this lesson's real 513.6% number does without softening it, is to make the real cost of past incidents visible, not to reset the count whenever it's inconvenient.

Write one sentence on whether the real percentage got better, worse, or stayed about the same, and why that makes sense given when this course's real outages were actually injected relative to now.

docs.title: Burn Rate Alerts: Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting
What was run
docs.text: Real burn rate — how many times faster than sustainable the error budget from Lesson 2 is being consumed — computed from this course's own real, live traffic at two different real window lengths: a long 1-hour window (still reflecting this course's real past outages) and a short, very recent window, to see whether they agree.

docs.title: The real burn rate, two real windows, two real different pictures
docs.text:
burn_rate = error_ratio / (1 - slo_target)      # slo_target = 0.95, so budget = 0.05

# long window: 1 hour
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1h])) / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1h]))'
# 0.25680069927491816   -> burn rate = 0.2568 / 0.05 = 5.136x

# short window: 1 minute
curl -s ".../api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status!="200"}[1m])) / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[1m]))'
# NaN   -> no real traffic at all in the last minute

The real long window still shows a burn rate of 5.136x — a real, genuine reflection of this course's past injected outages, still inside the 1-hour lookback. The real short window shows NaN — literally no real checkout traffic has happened recently enough to even compute a ratio. These two real numbers tell two different, both-true stories: "there was a real, severe problem within the last hour" (long window) and "nothing is actively happening right this second" (short window) — and an alert that only looked at one of them would get an incomplete, potentially misleading picture.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A single-window burn-rate alert has a real, structural tradeoff no single window length escapes: a short window (reacts fast, but trusts a tiny, noisy sample — a handful of real requests can swing the ratio wildly) or a long window (statistically stable, but exactly as this lesson's real 5.136x shows, keeps reporting a problem for the entire window's duration even after the real underlying issue has completely stopped, because old, real, already-resolved failures are still inside the lookback).

Multi-window burn-rate alerting (the real pattern Google's SRE workbook popularized) fixes both problems at once by requiring both a long window AND a short window to show an elevated burn rate before firing: the long window confirms the problem is real and statistically meaningful, not just a noisy blip; the short window confirms it's still actively happening right now, not an issue from earlier in the long window that's already resolved — precisely the real distinction this lesson's two actual numbers (5.136x long, NaN/quiet short) make directly visible. A real multi-window rule combining both might require, for example, a 1-hour burn rate above 5x and a 5-minute burn rate above 5x before paging — satisfied by neither of this lesson's two real numbers alone, which is exactly the correct, non-noisy outcome given that nothing is actively failing right now.

This also typically comes with multiple burn-rate thresholds, not just one: a very high burn rate (say, 14x, meaning the entire 30-day budget would be exhausted in about 2 days at the current rate) justifies an immediate page; a lower, sustained burn rate (say, 3x, exhausting the budget in about 10 days) might only justify a ticket for the next business day — the same page-vs-ticket severity split Level 2, Lesson 5 built directly, now driven by how fast the budget is being spent rather than a flat threshold.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Alerting on a single window length and accepting either its noise (too short) or its staleness (too long) as an unavoidable tradeoff — multi-window alerting exists specifically because this tradeoff doesn't have to be accepted; combining two windows gets the benefit of both.
  • Treating a long-window burn rate as "currently happening" without checking a short window — this lesson's real numbers show exactly how misleading that would be: a real 5.136x long-window burn rate with genuinely zero current traffic.
  • Using the same burn-rate threshold for every severity level instead of a real tiered system (fast-and-severe pages immediately, slow-and-sustained becomes a lower-urgency ticket) — collapsing every burn rate into one alert reintroduces the alert-fatigue risk Level 2, Lesson 6 measured directly.

docs.title: Designing an SLO for a Real Service
What was run
docs.text: Real p50, p95, and p99 checkout latency computed from this course's own actual historical Prometheus data — an attempt to use it as a real baseline for designing an SLO, which surfaced a real, honest problem with the data itself before any SLO could be responsibly chosen.

docs.title: The real numbers, and the real problem with them
docs.text:
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum(rate(orders_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint="/checkout"}[1h])) by (le))
# 0.0927364864864865
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(orders_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint="/checkout"}[1h])) by (le))
# 2.29875
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(orders_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint="/checkout"}[1h])) by (le))
# 2.45975

p50 is a real, reasonable 93ms. p95 and p99 jump to a real 2.3–2.46 seconds — a real, honest red flag, but not about the service's actual normal behavior. Rather than assume a cause, the real high-latency samples were located precisely with a real query_range scan: two genuine spikes to ~2.48 seconds, both timestamped within a two-minute window. Checking what this course was actually doing at that exact real time identified the cause: Lesson 6's real burst of 300 concurrent checkout requests, sent all at once via threading to measure absolute-vs-ratio alerting. That real burst genuinely saturated the app's request-handling thread pool, and a handful of real requests queued for seconds waiting for a free worker — a real, unintentional side effect of that lesson's own test traffic, still sitting inside this 1-hour lookback window. Designing a real SLO from this data as-is would mean committing to a latency target inflated by that deliberate stress-test burst, not the service's real, organic behavior.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Designing a real SLO starts with a real baseline — but "real data" and "representative data" are not the same thing, and this lesson's own numbers show exactly how they can diverge. A genuinely responsible SLO design process has to actively exclude or account for known-artificial periods (deliberate chaos tests, known incidents already being fixed, deployment windows with expected elevated error rates) before trusting raw historical percentiles as "what normal looks like." Skipping this step — taking p95=2.3s at face value — would either commit to an unnecessarily loose SLO (giving up real headroom to detect genuine future degradation) or, worse, bake a known test artifact into a number treated as a real production commitment.

With that caveat made explicit, the real, practical SLO design process:

  1. Establish a real, clean baseline — p50 of 93ms here is a plausible, uncontaminated number (fast operations aren't much affected by one slow tail event skewing a high percentile), and would need to be re-measured over a longer, cleaner window for p95/p99 specifically.
  2. Choose a target with real headroom above the baseline, not equal to it — an SLO set exactly at current measured performance leaves no room for natural variance and will be breached by routine noise; a common real practice is targeting something the service already beats most of the time, so the SLO represents a genuine commitment with margin, not a coin flip.
  3. Choose a real, specific time window — Lesson 1's distinction between a raw SLI and an SLO applies directly here: "p95 latency under 500ms, measured over a rolling 28 days" is a real SLO; "p95 latency under 500ms" with no window is not fully specified.
  4. Validate the target is actually achievable against real, clean historical data — exactly what this lesson's contaminated numbers prevented from being done responsibly without first addressing the data quality issue found.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Designing an SLO from raw historical data without checking it for exactly the kind of contamination this lesson found — a known chaos test, an incident window, or a deployment spike can silently distort a percentile enough to produce a misleadingly loose (or, in other cases, misleadingly tight) target.
  • Setting an SLO target with zero real margin above current measured performance, leaving no room for ordinary variance to avoid constant, false SLO breaches.
  • Designing an SLO once and never revisiting it as the real service's behavior and real traffic patterns change — a baseline from months ago may no longer represent what "normal" actually looks like today.

Report the real, clean p95 latency this produces, and use it to propose one specific, real, properly-justified SLO target and window for orders_app.py's /checkout endpoint.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real capacity projection built directly from this course's own live Prometheus TSDB status — its real current series count, real elapsed time, and real on-disk size — extrapolated forward the naive way first, then corrected once the real cause of the naive projection's error was identified.

docs.title: The real, naive projection — and why it's real but wrong
docs.text:
curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/status/tsdb"
# headStats.numSeries: 5223
# minTime -> maxTime spans 73.2 real minutes


rate_per_min = 5223 / 73.2   # 71.35 series/min, a real observed average

projected at this rate:
  24 hours: 102737 series
  7 days:   719161 series

A real, honestly-computed linear projection — and almost certainly wrong as a forecast of genuine future growth. The real cause: this course's own cardinality demonstrations (Level 1, Lesson 8's 2,000-series app, Level 3, Lesson 7's 500-series cardinality bomb) each added a real, one-time burst of thousands of series in minutes, not a sustained, ongoing growth rate — the exact same "contaminated baseline" problem Lesson 4 found for latency percentiles, now showing up in capacity planning instead.

docs.title: The real, honest per-series storage cost — a genuinely more durable number
docs.text:
du -sh prom-data   # 4.7M

bytes_per_series = 4.7 * 1024 * 1024 / 5223   # 943.6 bytes/series

real storage per series so far: 943.6 bytes/series
projected storage at 100,000 series: 90.0 MB

This real ratio — storage cost per series, not per unit time — is a more durable, reusable number than the time-based growth rate above, because it doesn't depend on assuming this course's artificial test bursts represent real, ongoing traffic growth. It can be recombined with a genuinely trustworthy growth estimate (from actual, steady-state production traffic trends, not a test artifact) to produce a real, defensible storage forecast.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Real capacity planning for an observability system — disk space for Prometheus's TSDB, query load, ingestion throughput — depends on getting the growth rate right, and this lesson's own naive 719,161-series week-ahead projection shows exactly how a short observation window can badly mislead that estimate if it happens to include one-time artifacts (a deliberate cardinality test, a migration, a temporary debug flag someone forgot to remove) rather than steady-state behavior. The real, practical fix mirrors Lesson 4's: separate durable, reusable ratios (bytes per series, bytes per sample — properties of the storage engine and data shape, relatively stable over time) from time-based growth rates (series added per minute — highly sensitive to whatever happened to be running during the observation window), and be skeptical of any capacity forecast built primarily on the latter without first checking whether the observation window was representative.

A genuinely sound real capacity plan combines: (1) a real, validated per-unit cost (this lesson's 943.6 bytes/series, or an equivalent per-sample ingestion cost), with (2) a real, trustworthy growth projection — ideally derived from multiple longer observation windows, explicitly excluding or separately accounting for known one-time events, cross-checked against whatever is actually planned (more services being onboarded, more instances being deployed) rather than extrapolated blindly from whatever the monitoring system happened to see during one arbitrary recent window.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Extrapolating linearly from a short observation window without checking whether anything unusual (a test, a migration, an incident) happened during that specific window — this lesson's own real 7-day projection is a direct, measured example of exactly this mistake.
  • Conflating a durable per-unit cost (bytes per series) with a time-based growth rate (series per minute) — the first is a relatively stable property of the system; the second is only as reliable as the window it was measured over, as shown here.
  • Planning capacity for the current moment's scale with no margin, rather than for a real, validated projection of where the system will be by the time any new capacity actually gets provisioned and deployed.

Compare it directly to this lesson's original 71.35 series/min figure, and report how much lower the real, steady-state rate is once the contaminating test bursts are no longer part of the observation window.

docs.title: Scaling Prometheus: Federation, Remote Write & Long-Term Storage
What was run
docs.text: No new experiment — this lesson picks up directly from Lesson 5's real, validated 943.6 bytes/series storage cost and asks the honest next question: what actually happens once a real system's series count and retention requirements outgrow what one Prometheus server, on one machine, can reasonably hold — and what are the real, documented architectures for that, since this course's single-laptop scope never required running any of them.

docs.title: The real number that eventually forces this question
docs.text:
real storage per series so far: 943.6 bytes/series

A single Prometheus server, as this entire course has run it, keeps all its data on one local disk, served by one process. At 943.6 bytes/series, even this lesson's deliberately modest 5,223-series lab instance used real, measured megabytes — scale that out to a production system monitoring hundreds of real services, each with dozens of real metrics and real label combinations, over months of real retention, and the honest arithmetic stops fitting on one machine's disk, long before it stops fitting in one machine's query performance budget.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Three real, standard architectures address this, each solving a different real limitation of a single Prometheus server — none of them run in this course, stated plainly, since every earlier lesson's real verification depended specifically on a single, directly-inspectable local instance:

  • Federation: one Prometheus server scrapes aggregated data from other Prometheus servers (via their own /federate endpoint), rather than scraping every individual target directly. This lets a top-level server hold a rolled-up, cross-cluster view without needing every raw series from every underlying server — real for building a "global" dashboard across multiple independently-run Prometheus instances, but it doesn't solve the single-server retention or raw-data-volume problem for any one of those underlying servers; it's a query aggregation answer, not a storage scaling answer.
  • Remote write: a Prometheus server forwards every real scraped sample, as it's ingested, to a separate, external storage system over a standard remote-write protocol, instead of (or in addition to) keeping it in its own local TSDB. This decouples ingestion and local short-term querying (which Prometheus keeps doing exactly as this course has run it) from long-term storage and cross-server querying (handled by whatever system is on the receiving end), directly solving the local-disk retention limit this lesson's own real per-series cost points toward.
  • Long-term storage systems (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir — all real, widely-used, explicitly not run in this course) typically consume remote-written data from many Prometheus servers, storing it in cheaper, more scalable backends (often real object storage like S3) while still exposing a Prometheus-compatible query API — letting real PromQL, the exact language every lesson in this course has used directly, keep working unchanged against a system that scales far beyond what one local TSDB could.

The real, honest thread connecting all three to this course: every one of them exists specifically to solve the exact problem this lesson's own real numbers made concrete — one server's local disk and one server's query engine eventually can't hold or serve a real production system's full retention and cardinality needs, and each architecture solves a different piece of "where does the data actually live, long-term" without requiring a return to re-deriving PromQL, metric types, or instrumentation practice from scratch; everything built across Levels 1–3 remains directly applicable on top of whichever of these a real team chooses.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reaching for Thanos/Cortex/Mimir before a real, measured need exists — every one of these adds real operational complexity (another distributed system to run and understand) that a single Prometheus server, correctly sized using the real methodology from Lesson 5, may not need for a long time.
  • Treating federation as a solution to a storage-scaling problem — as described above, it's fundamentally a cross-server query aggregation mechanism, not a way to reduce any individual server's own real storage burden.
  • Assuming "scaling Prometheus" always means more infrastructure, without first applying the real, cheaper levers this course already built directly — fixing a real cardinality problem (Level 3, Lesson 7), using recording rules to reduce real repeated query cost (Level 1, Lesson 8), and sampling where applicable (Level 3, Lesson 5) can each meaningfully delay or reduce the real need for a bigger architecture.

Write down, specifically, which of the three architectures above you'd reach for first at that real projected scale, and why — grounded in the actual numbers you've computed, not a general impression of what "big" observability systems use.

docs.title: Observability as Code: Dashboards & Alerts in Version Control
What was run
docs.text: The real RED dashboard from Level 2, Lesson 2 was exported as real JSON from Grafana's own API, committed to a real local git repository, modified with a real new panel added programmatically, diffed with real git diff, and pushed back to the live Grafana instance through the same API — with the real result confirmed both by Grafana's own version number and by actually loading the dashboard in a browser.

docs.title: The real round trip, start to finish
docs.text:
curl -s "http://admin:admin@localhost:3000/api/dashboards/uid/afmstj" | python3 -c "
import json, sys
json.dump(json.load(sys.stdin)['dashboard'], open('red_dashboard.json', 'w'), indent=2)
"

A real, new panel was then added directly to the JSON file — no clicking through Grafana's UI — and the real change was inspected with git diff before anything was pushed anywhere:

+    {
+      "id": 4,
+      "type": "stat",
+      "title": "Current in-flight requests",
+      ...

# the modified, version-controlled JSON pushed back through the real API:
curl -X POST ".../api/dashboards/db" -d '{"dashboard": {...}, "overwrite": true}'
# {"status":"success", "uid":"afmstj", "version":2}

Loading the real dashboard in a browser afterward showed a real fourth panel, "Current in-flight requests," live and rendering real data — exactly the change that was visible in the git diff beforehand, with nothing lost or silently altered in the round trip from Grafana, to a file, to git, and back to Grafana.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every dashboard, alert rule, and recording rule in this entire course has existed as real, plain-text configuration from the start — this lesson's contribution isn't a new tool, it's the discipline of treating that configuration the way any other real source code is treated: committed to version control, changed through real, reviewable diffs, and deployed through a repeatable, automatable process rather than manual clicks inside a UI that leave no record of what changed or why.

The real, concrete benefits this round trip demonstrates directly: a real diff (the git diff above) shows exactly what changed, reviewable by a second person before it's ever applied to the live system — something a screenshot of a UI change before-and-after can't offer with the same precision. A real commit history becomes a genuine audit trail: who changed this dashboard, when, and why, recoverable months later. And a real, repeatable apply step (the same POST .../api/dashboards/db call, scriptable and automatable) means recreating this exact dashboard on a fresh Grafana instance — a disaster recovery scenario, a new environment, a teammate's local setup — is a matter of replaying committed JSON, not manually recreating every panel by memory.

This same discipline applies identically to the real prometheus.yml, alert_rules.yml, and recording_rules.yml files this course has built and modified throughout Levels 1–4 — every one of them is already real, version-controllable text, and the real workflow this lesson demonstrated for a Grafana dashboard (export or author as code, diff, apply via a real API or config reload, verify live) applies without modification to all of them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Making dashboard or alert changes directly in a UI with no corresponding commit, leaving no real record of what changed, when, or why — exactly the gap this lesson's git diff-first workflow closes.
  • Committing exported JSON without first checking it for environment-specific values (a real datasource UID, like ag2egat7m3l6oe in this lesson's own example, is specific to this Grafana instance) — re-applying it verbatim to a different environment without adjusting those values would silently point panels at the wrong, or a nonexistent, data source.
  • Treating "observability as code" as only covering dashboards — alert rules, recording rules, and scrape configs are equally real, equally version-controllable, and arguably more consequential to get a reviewed diff on before deploying, exactly as Level 2, Lesson 10's real alert-rule bug demonstrated the cost of an unreviewed change.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Commit this course's real alert_rules.yml to the same git repository, make a real, deliberate change to one threshold, and inspect the real diff before applying it. Then write a small real script that reloads Prometheus's configuration from disk (restarting the process, since this course's setup doesn't have the lifecycle API enabled) and confirms, via /api/v1/rules, that the real new threshold is actually in effect — completing the same real export-diff-apply-verify loop this lesson built for dashboards, now for alert rules instead.

docs.title: On-Call & Incident Response With Your Own Stack
What was run
docs.text: One complete, real incident, worked end to end using only this course's own real stack: a real outage injected into payments_service.py, detected by the real burn-rate-style alert from Level 2, Lesson 10, diagnosed using real PromQL and real structured logs, mitigated, and verified resolved — with every real timestamp recorded as it actually happened, including an honest, unplanned finding about how long real recovery actually took.

docs.title: The real timeline, as it actually happened
docs.text:
T+0s   (15:15:21) real incident injected: curl -X POST .../incident/true
T+1s   (15:15:22) real traffic sent during the incident
T+23s  (15:15:44) real page received: [PAGER] status=firing alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRatio

Detection took 23 real seconds — the alert's for: 10s debounce plus Alertmanager's real group_wait delay, both real, deliberate design choices from Level 2, not unexplained latency.

T+23s  real diagnosis: checkout error ratio = 1 (100% failing)
T+23s  real structured log: {"reason": "declined: card processor unavailable", "status": 402}
T+29s  (15:15:50) real mitigation: curl -X POST .../incident/false
T+30s  real recovery traffic sent

T+80s  (15:16:41) alert FINALLY cleared, after a SECOND round of real recovery traffic
T+80s  real resolved page received: [PAGER] status=resolved alertname=HighCheckoutErrorRatio

The real, honest, unplanned finding: fixing the root cause at T+29s did not immediately clear the alert. The first batch of real recovery traffic (10 requests) left the real 1-minute ratio window still mixed with enough recent bad data to stay above the 0.5 threshold (value: 0.6667, confirmed directly) — it took a second, larger batch of real clean traffic before the ratio genuinely dropped and the alert cleared, a full 51 real seconds after the actual fix was applied.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's real timeline makes concrete every piece built across this course, used together under real pressure: the real alert (Level 2) detected the problem; real PromQL (Level 1) and real structured logs (Level 2) diagnosed it precisely — the log line named the exact real reason, "card processor unavailable," within seconds of the page arriving; the real fix was applied directly at the source; and the real alert's own eventual clearing served as objective, automated confirmation that the fix actually worked, rather than relying on a human's subjective sense that things seemed better.

The real, honest gap between mitigation (T+29s) and the alert actually clearing (T+80s) is not a flaw in this course's alerting design — it's a genuine, important property of ratio-based, windowed alerts that a real on-call engineer needs to understand: the alert's condition is evaluated over a real time window (1 minute here), so a real fix doesn't retroactively erase the bad data already inside that window. Declaring an incident "resolved" the moment a fix is applied, without waiting for the real alert to confirm, risks closing out an incident that isn't actually confirmed fixed yet — exactly the gap this lesson's real 51-second delay makes concrete rather than theoretical.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Declaring an incident resolved the instant a fix is applied, without waiting for the real monitoring signal to independently confirm it — this lesson's real 51-second gap between "fix applied" and "alert actually cleared" is exactly the kind of premature closure this habit risks.
  • Skipping the diagnosis step and guessing at a fix based on the alert name alone — this lesson's real structured log (naming the specific real reason, "card processor unavailable") was available within seconds and made the real root cause unambiguous, rather than requiring guesswork.
  • Treating every real incident's recovery time as instant, the way a dashboard's "all green now" status might casually imply — a ratio-based or windowed alert's real recovery time depends on real, fresh traffic flowing through the window, which can genuinely lag behind the real moment the underlying fix was applied.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's exact real incident scenario, but this time measure precisely how much real clean traffic (by request count, not just elapsed time) is needed before the alert clears, holding traffic rate roughly constant. Report the real number, and use it to estimate, for a real production service with a known real request rate, how long a similar ratio-based alert would take to confirm recovery after a real fix — a genuinely useful number for setting on-call expectations about "how long until the page actually stops."

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: No new experiment — this lesson tallies the real anti-patterns this course caught directly, in its own real data, across every earlier level, as the concrete evidence base for the patterns worth naming and avoiding deliberately.

docs.title: The real anti-patterns, each one caught with real evidence
docs.text: Anti-pattern Caught in Real evidence Trusting a raw counter without rate() Level 1, Lesson 6 A real restart dropped a counter from 53 to 5; a naive (last-first)/duration would have shown a nonsensical negative rate Unbounded label cardinality Level 3, Lesson 7 500 real requests with a UUID label created 500 real series and 37,000 bytes, vs. 1 series and 26 bytes done correctly Averaging already-computed percentiles Level 1, Lesson 7 A naive average of two real instances' p95s gave 0.509s; the real, correctly-aggregated p95 was 0.9415s Alerting on absolute thresholds instead of ratios Level 2, Lesson 6 A real absolute-rate alert fired on genuinely healthy traffic (92.7% real success) Shallow black-box health checks Level 3, Lesson 9 /health returned real 200 healthy during a real 100%-failure outage Single-window alerting Level 4, Lesson 3 A real long-window burn rate of 5.136x coexisted with a real short-window NaN (zero current traffic) Unreviewed PromQL precedence bugs Level 2, Lesson 10 A real alert rule silently never fired, health: ok the whole time, due to an unparenthesized and/> Contaminated baselines for SLOs and capacity Level 4, Lessons 4–5 Real p95 latency inflated to 2.3s by an old test; a real naive growth projection overestimated by including one-time test bursts Trusting that work completed without independent confirmation Level 4, Lesson 8 A real fix at T+29s didn't clear the real alert until T+80s — the alert, not the fix timestamp, was the real signal that mattered Assuming a networking primitive works without testing it Level 1, Lesson 4, Level 3, Lesson 3 A suspected Prometheus scraping bug turned out fine when actually tested; a real start_http_server() genuinely failed in this environment when actually tested

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every row in this table is the same real, general lesson applied to a different specific mechanism: a plausible assumption about an observability system's behavior is not the same as a verified fact about it, and this course's own real, repeated experience — across metrics, alerting, tracing, and SLOs — is that the gap between the two shows up constantly, in both directions. Sometimes the assumption was too pessimistic (the suspected redirect bug in Level 1, Lesson 4 turned out not to matter). Sometimes it was too optimistic (the start_http_server() assumption in Level 3, Lesson 3 turned out to be genuinely broken in this specific environment). Sometimes a real, syntactically valid rule was silently, invisibly wrong (Level 2, Lesson 10). The common thread across every real example in this table isn't any one specific technology — it's that each one was caught only because this course tested the actual behavior directly against real data, rather than trusting what seemed reasonable.

The second, related thread: several of these anti-patterns (Lessons 4–5 especially) show that even real, genuinely-measured data can mislead if it isn't checked for what it actually represents — raw numbers from a system under test, a known incident, or a deliberately injected fault are real, but not necessarily representative of the steady-state behavior a real SLO or capacity plan needs to be built on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading this list as "things that can theoretically go wrong" rather than "things this course's own real data actually demonstrated going wrong" — every single row has a real, specific, reproducible example attached, not a hypothetical one.
  • Assuming familiarity with these patterns in the abstract is the same as catching them in a real, specific system — every one of these was only caught here by running real experiments against real data, not by knowing the pattern existed in general.
  • Treating this as a complete list — it's a tally of what this specific course's specific real experiments happened to surface, not an exhaustive catalog of every possible observability anti-pattern.

Write down one specific, real check you could run today against that real system — not hypothetically, an actual command or query you could execute — to find out whether that same anti-pattern is present, the same way every row in this table was found: by testing directly, not by assuming.

docs.title: Capstone: Build a Complete SLO-Driven Observability Stack
What was run
docs.text: Every real piece this course built, running together, one final time: the real orders_app.py and payments_service.py from Level 1, the real Prometheus server and alert rules from Levels 1–2, the real Alertmanager and pager from Level 2, the real structured logs and traces from Levels 2–3, and a real, final Grafana dashboard (Checkout SLO Dashboard) built specifically to show this course's own real SLO status, live.

docs.title: The real, final, live result
docs.text:
# SLI panel
sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status="200"}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[5m]))

# error budget consumed panel (against a 95% SLO)

     / sum(rate(orders_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout"}[5m])))) / 0.05) * 100

Loaded live in a real browser, this dashboard rendered:

  • Real SLI: 0.887 — 88.7% of real checkouts succeeding, right now, in this real 5-minute window.
  • Real error budget consumed: 226%, in bright red — this course's real cumulative traffic, including every deliberately injected real outage across all four levels, has spent more than double a real 95% SLO's entire allowance.
  • A real SLI-over-time graph, visibly dropping to near-zero during this course's own real incidents (the Level 2 and Level 4 outage injections) and recovering afterward — a real, honest, visual record of this course's own testing history, not a staged example.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This dashboard is not a new mechanism — it's the direct, combined application of this entire course's real building blocks to one specific, real operational question: is this service meeting its reliability target right now, and by how much is it over or under budget? The SLI panel is a real PromQL ratio query (Level 1). The budget panel is that same real ratio, transformed by the real error-budget arithmetic from Lesson 2. The time-series panel is the real Grafana visualization mechanics from Level 2, Lesson 1. The real 226% figure sitting behind it all is backed by a real alert rule (Level 2, Lesson 10), real structured logs explaining each real failure (Level 2, Lesson 8), and real traces that could pinpoint exactly where in a multi-service chain any one of them happened (Level 3, Lesson 6).

The real, honest number this capstone ends on — 226% of budget consumed, visibly, in red — is not a clean, reassuring finish, and that's deliberate and true to how this course actually ran: forty lessons of genuine, repeated fault injection, real alert testing, and real incident simulation leave real, visible marks on a real system's real reliability numbers, exactly as they would on an actual production system that had been through a comparably eventful few days. An SLO-driven observability stack's job isn't to make that number look good — it's to make it honestly, precisely visible, which is exactly what this real dashboard does.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building an impressive-looking dashboard without the underlying real alerting, logging, and tracing to back it up — this capstone's dashboard is only meaningful because every number on it traces back to a real, verified mechanism built and tested across the previous 39 lessons, not because the panels themselves look convincing.
  • Treating a bad real SLO number (like this lesson's real 226%) as something to hide or explain away rather than the honest, actionable signal it is — the whole point of tracking it this precisely is to make it impossible to ignore.
  • Considering observability "done" once a dashboard exists — this course's real, repeated finding, across every level, is that building the instrumentation is necessary but not sufficient; it only becomes useful once it's actually tested against real failures, exactly as this capstone's dashboard was.
